title: Candidate keys and alternate keys
description: A practical guide to separating all possible row identifiers from the one chosen as the primary key, using a hypothetical customer table with counterexamples.
lead: Candidate keys are the identifiers that could uniquely name rows in a relation. The primary key is the candidate key you choose to use as the main identifier. Alternate keys are the remaining candidate keys you still want the model to respect. The distinction matters because a table can have several valid identifiers, but only one should carry the job of being the default reference point for joins, foreign keys, and human reasoning.

sections.heading: The short version
paragraphs: A superkey is any set of attributes that uniquely identifies a row. A candidate key is a minimal superkey: it is unique, and no attribute can be removed without losing uniqueness. A primary key is the candidate key selected as the table’s principal identifier. An alternate key is a candidate key that was not selected as primary.

This is a modeling distinction before it is an implementation detail. A database can enforce primary key and unique constraints, but the modeler still has to decide which facts are stable enough to be identifiers and which facts only look unique in today’s sample data.

For example, a customer table might have a generated customer_id, an email address, and a loyalty_card_number. If all three are unique and required by the business rules, each may be a candidate key. If the model chooses customer_id as the primary key, then email and loyalty_card_number become alternate keys. If email can be reused, missing, shared, or corrected, it is not a candidate key even if it is unique in a small extract.
bullets: Superkey: any unique row identifier, possibly with extra columns.
Candidate key: a minimal superkey.
Primary key: the candidate key chosen as the main identifier.
Alternate key: a candidate key not chosen as primary.

sections.heading: A hypothetical customer fixture
paragraphs: Use this small hypothetical retail customer relation. The goal is not to design a complete customer model. The goal is to separate possible identifiers from the selected identifier.

Assume the intended relation is one row per registered customer. The business has assigned each customer a stable internal customer_id. Each registered customer must have exactly one account_email and one loyalty_card_number. For this fixture, both account_email and loyalty_card_number are required to be unique among registered customers.

Under those assumptions, three single-column attributes identify a customer: customer_id, account_email, and loyalty_card_number. Each is unique. Each is minimal because no smaller subset exists than one column. Therefore, each is a candidate key. If the data model chooses customer_id as the primary key, then account_email and loyalty_card_number are alternate keys.

The phrase ‘under those assumptions’ is doing real work. Candidate keys come from semantics, not from a lucky profile of one dataset. If emails are allowed to change, they can still be an alternate key for the current customer table if the rule is ‘current email is unique and required.’ If email history is stored in the same relation, email probably stops identifying one current customer row. If loyalty cards can be missing or reassigned, loyalty_card_number is not a candidate key for this relation.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative PostgreSQL 18-style DDL for the hypothetical fixture.
-- This is a modeling example, not an execution result.

CREATE TABLE registered_customer (
    customer_id          integer PRIMARY KEY,
    account_email        text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    loyalty_card_number  text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    full_name            text NOT NULL,
    signup_date          date NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO registered_customer
    (customer_id, account_email, loyalty_card_number, full_name, signup_date)
VALUES
    (101, 'a Rivera@example.test', 'LC-7001', 'Avery Rivera', DATE '2026-01-04'),
    (102, 'b Shah@example.test',    'LC-7002', 'Blair Shah',   DATE '2026-01-05'),
    (103, 'c Morgan@example.test',  'LC-7003', 'Casey Morgan', DATE '2026-01-07');

sections.heading: Counterexamples that look like keys
paragraphs: Many modeling errors start when a column is treated as a key because it is unique in a sample. The sample may be clean, incomplete, or too small to show the real rule. Here are four common counterexamples using the same hypothetical customer context.

First, full_name is not a key. In the three-row fixture, full_name happens to be unique. But names do not identify registered customers under normal retail assumptions. Two customers can share the same name, and one customer can change a name. Uniqueness in the current rows is not enough.

Second, signup_date is not a key. It is not unique in the intended domain. Even if this sample has different dates, many customers can sign up on the same date. A date may help describe a customer; it does not identify one.

Third, customer_id plus account_email is a superkey but not a candidate key. The pair is unique because customer_id is already unique. However, account_email can be removed and the remaining customer_id still identifies the row. That makes the pair non-minimal. It is a superkey with an unnecessary passenger.

Fourth, account_email may fail as a candidate key if the business rule changes. Suppose guest checkout rows, family accounts, or historical email records are added to the same relation. If account_email can be null, shared, or repeated over time, it is not a candidate key for that relation. It may belong in a separate relation with its own grain and validity rules.
bullets: A column that is unique in a sample is only a candidate key if the business rule guarantees uniqueness for the relation.
Adding extra columns to an already unique identifier creates a superkey, not a candidate key.
A descriptive attribute can be important for analytics while still being invalid as an identifier.
When the grain changes, old keys may stop being keys.

codeExamples.code:
-- Diagnostic queries for the hypothetical fixture.
-- These queries find duplicate values in possible single-column identifiers.
-- A zero-row result is necessary evidence, but not sufficient proof, of a candidate key.

SELECT account_email, COUNT(*) AS row_count
FROM registered_customer
GROUP BY account_email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

SELECT loyalty_card_number, COUNT(*) AS row_count
FROM registered_customer
GROUP BY loyalty_card_number
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

SELECT full_name, COUNT(*) AS row_count
FROM registered_customer
GROUP BY full_name
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

sections.heading: How to classify possible identifiers
paragraphs: A practical way to classify identifiers is to start with the relation’s grain, then test each possible identifier against uniqueness, minimality, requiredness, and stability. These checks are conceptual first. Data profiling can reveal violations, but it cannot by itself define the business rule.

Step one: state the grain. For the example table, the grain is one row per registered customer. Without this sentence, the key conversation is ambiguous. An email may identify a current registered customer, an email address record, a login credential, or a message recipient depending on the table.

Step two: list plausible identifiers. In the hypothetical fixture, the plausible identifiers are customer_id, account_email, and loyalty_card_number. Less plausible attributes such as full_name and signup_date can still be examined, but they should not be promoted merely because they look unique today.

Step three: check uniqueness against the intended domain. A key must identify at most one row. If the organization allows two registered customers to share an email address, account_email is not a candidate key. If it does not allow sharing, and the table stores only the current email for each registered customer, then account_email can be a candidate key.

Step four: check requiredness. In relational key theory, key attributes identify tuples; in SQL implementations, nullable unique columns need special attention. PostgreSQL documentation describes primary key constraints as enforcing both uniqueness and not-null behavior. It also documents unique constraints, where null handling is a separate concern. Practically, if a supposed key can be missing, it is not a reliable identifier for the relation unless the design explicitly handles that case.

Step five: check minimality. If customer_id alone identifies a row, then customer_id plus account_email is not a candidate key. It is still unique, but it is not minimal. Minimality prevents bloated identifiers that make foreign keys wider and obscure the real dependency.

Step six: select one primary key. The selected primary key should be stable, compact enough to reference, and aligned with how dependent tables will point to this relation. The other candidate keys do not disappear. They remain alternate keys and should be documented and, where appropriate, constrained.

sections.heading: Primary key choice does not erase alternate keys
paragraphs: Choosing customer_id as the primary key does not mean account_email and loyalty_card_number are unimportant. It means customer_id is the identifier the model uses as the principal reference. Alternate keys still express business rules: no two registered customers can have the same current account email, and no two registered customers can have the same loyalty card number.

This distinction prevents two opposite mistakes. The first mistake is using every unique field as if it were the primary key. That leads to inconsistent joins: one pipeline joins orders to customers by customer_id, another joins events by email, and a third joins rewards activity by loyalty card. When the values change or arrive late, the model has no single anchor.

The second mistake is enforcing only the primary key and ignoring alternate keys. If customer_id is unique but account_email is allowed to duplicate accidentally, the table may still satisfy its primary key constraint while violating the business rule that each current account email belongs to one registered customer. The primary key protects row identity; alternate keys protect other valid identifiers.

In SQL, a common implementation is a primary key constraint for the selected key and unique constraints for alternate keys. That maps well to the concept but is not the whole design. The model should also record what the alternate key means: current email, verified email, login email, billing email, active loyalty card, or something else. Without that meaning, the constraint name may be correct while the data model remains unclear.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative implementation of one primary key and two alternate keys.
-- Constraint names make the modeling decision explicit.

CREATE TABLE registered_customer (
    customer_id          integer NOT NULL,
    account_email        text NOT NULL,
    loyalty_card_number  text NOT NULL,
    full_name            text NOT NULL,
    signup_date          date NOT NULL,

    CONSTRAINT pk_registered_customer
        PRIMARY KEY (customer_id),

    CONSTRAINT ak_registered_customer_account_email
        UNIQUE (account_email),

    CONSTRAINT ak_registered_customer_loyalty_card_number
        UNIQUE (loyalty_card_number)
);

sections.heading: Join semantics and foreign keys
paragraphs: Keys also shape how tables relate. Suppose a hypothetical order table has one row per order and stores customer_id. A foreign key from customer_order.customer_id to registered_customer.customer_id says each order references the selected customer identifier. The join condition follows the modeled relationship, not whichever customer attribute happens to be available in an event feed.

If an upstream source supplies only account_email, that does not make account_email the primary key. It means the ingestion process may need to resolve account_email to customer_id using the alternate key. The alternate key is useful precisely because it gives a safe lookup path while preserving customer_id as the table’s primary reference.

This is where candidate keys and alternate keys become practical for data engineering. They make joins intentional. Joining orders to customers on full_name is invalid even if a profiling query shows no duplicate names today. Joining on account_email can be valid if account_email is an enforced alternate key and the business meaning is current customer email. Joining on customer_id is usually preferred when the dependent table already carries that primary identifier.

The rule is simple: a join key should match a declared relationship or a declared alternate identifier, not a coincidental attribute. PostgreSQL’s table expression documentation describes joins as deriving rows from related table expressions, but the database cannot infer your business grain from a join predicate alone. The data model has to supply that meaning.

codeExamples.code:
-- Hypothetical dependent table using the selected primary identifier.

CREATE TABLE customer_order (
    order_id     integer PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id  integer NOT NULL,
    order_date   date NOT NULL,
    order_total  numeric(10,2) NOT NULL,

    CONSTRAINT fk_customer_order_registered_customer
        FOREIGN KEY (customer_id)
        REFERENCES registered_customer (customer_id)
);

-- If a source event arrives with only an email address, the alternate key can resolve it.
-- This is illustrative SQL, not an execution result.

SELECT
    e.source_event_id,
    c.customer_id,
    e.event_time
FROM source_email_event AS e
JOIN registered_customer AS c
  ON c.account_email = e.account_email;

sections.heading: A practical diagnostic for your own model
paragraphs: When reviewing a table, write down each possible identifier in four columns: unique, required, minimal, and stable for this relation. Then classify it as primary key, alternate key, non-minimal superkey, or not a key. This small exercise often exposes hidden grain problems.

For the hypothetical registered_customer relation, the diagnostic looks like this in prose. customer_id is unique, required, minimal, and stable, so it is a candidate key and the selected primary key. account_email is unique, required, and minimal under the stated rule, so it is a candidate key and an alternate key. loyalty_card_number is also a candidate key and an alternate key under the stated rule. customer_id plus account_email is unique but not minimal, so it is a superkey but not a candidate key. full_name is not guaranteed unique, so it is not a key. signup_date is not unique and not a key.

The most useful part of the diagnostic is not the label itself. It is the argument behind the label. If two engineers disagree about whether account_email is an alternate key, the disagreement should move to the rule: Can a registered customer lack an email? Can two customers share one? Are historical emails stored in this table? Can an email be reassigned to a different customer record? Once those questions are answered, the key classification usually becomes straightforward.

Do not let implementation shortcuts decide the model silently. A generated integer can be an excellent primary key, but it does not remove the need to constrain natural alternate identifiers. A natural identifier can be a valid primary key, but it should still be judged for stability and meaning. The core question is always the same: which attributes identify one row at this table’s grain, and which one will the model choose as the main reference?
bullets: Start with the table grain before naming keys.
Treat sample uniqueness as evidence to investigate, not as proof.
A primary key is selected from candidate keys; it is not the only possible identifier by definition.
Alternate keys should be documented and usually enforced when the database supports the rule.
Non-minimal unique combinations are superkeys, not candidate keys.

takeaways: Candidate keys are all minimal identifiers for a relation; the primary key is the one chosen as the principal identifier.
Alternate keys are not second-class data. They are candidate keys that still express business rules even though they were not selected as primary.
A unique-looking column is not automatically a key. It must match the table grain, be required, be unique by rule, and be minimal.
Adding columns to an already unique identifier creates a non-minimal superkey, not a better candidate key.
Use constraints and clear names to make primary and alternate key decisions visible in the schema.

title: Functional dependencies in analytical tables
description: Use functional dependency violations to find analytical attributes stored at the wrong grain, with a small hypothetical order-line dataset and an illustrative SQL diagnostic.
lead: Functional dependencies are a practical way to ask whether an attribute belongs at the grain where it is stored. In an analytical table, a violation often points to a column that is being treated as stable at one level of detail even though the data says it changes at another.

sections.heading: The grain question behind a dependency
paragraphs: A functional dependency says that one set of attributes determines another attribute. If customer_id determines customer_name, then every row with the same customer_id should have the same customer_name. If product_id determines product_category, then every row with the same product_id should have the same product_category. The useful part for data engineers is not the formal notation; it is the diagnostic question: when the same determinant has more than one dependent value, what grain is the dependent attribute really stored at?

Analytical tables commonly repeat descriptive attributes for convenience. A fact table at order-line grain may contain order_date, customer_id, product_id, customer_tier, product_category, and category_manager. Repetition alone is not a problem. A single order_date repeated across the lines of the same order may be intentional denormalization. The problem appears when the repeated attribute is interpreted as if it belongs to one grain, while the observed rows show that it varies at another.

This article assumes you already understand identifiers and selected keys. The focus here is narrower: use dependency violations as evidence that a descriptive attribute may be stored at the wrong grain, or that its determinant is missing part of the real business context.

sections.heading: A hypothetical order-line table
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical retail table named order_lines. Its declared analytical grain is one row per product sold on an order. In other words, order_id plus line_no identifies one row. The table repeats several descriptors so that analysts can group sales without joining dimensions.
Here is the fixture, shown as rows rather than as a fully designed model:
bullets: 1001, line 1, 2026-01-10, C001, Ada Lim, Silver, P10, Trail Helmet, Safety, Lee, quantity 1
1001, line 2, 2026-01-10, C001, Ada Lim, Silver, P11, Bike Light, Safety, Lee, quantity 2
1002, line 1, 2026-01-11, C002, Bo Chen, Bronze, P12, Water Bottle, Accessories, Nora, quantity 1
1003, line 1, 2026-02-05, C001, Ada Lim, Gold, P13, Floor Pump, Accessories, Nora, quantity 1
1004, line 1, 2026-02-08, C003, Cy Diaz, Silver, P11, Bike Light, Safety, Noor, quantity 1
1004, line 2, 2026-02-08, C003, Cy Diaz, Silver, P14, Gloves, Apparel, Mina, quantity 1
1005, line 1, 2026-02-09, C002, Bo Chen, Bronze, P12, Water Bottle, Accessories, Nora, quantity 2
1006, line 1, 2026-02-12, C004, Dee Park, Bronze, P15, Energy Bar, Accessories, Mina, quantity 5

sections.heading: Expected dependencies to test
paragraphs: Before writing checks, state the dependencies you believe should hold. This step matters because not every violation is a modeling defect. Some proposed dependencies are simply false business rules.
For the hypothetical table, these are plausible expectations:
bullets: order_id determines order_date and customer_id. All lines on the same order should belong to the same order header.
customer_id determines customer_name, assuming this table stores a stable customer display name and not a historical name snapshot.
product_id determines product_name, assuming product names are stable for the reporting period or are represented by a type 1-style descriptor.
product_id determines product_category, assuming each product is assigned to one category in this simplified fixture.
customer_id determines customer_tier only if tier is treated as a stable customer attribute. If tier can change over time, this dependency should not be expected.

category determines category_manager only if there is exactly one manager per category for the reporting period. If responsibility changes by date, region, or subcategory, category alone is not the correct determinant.

sections.heading: Illustrative SQL diagnostic
paragraphs: A dependency violation check groups by the determinant and counts the distinct dependent values. Any group with more than one dependent value is a counterexample to the proposed dependency.

The following is illustrative PostgreSQL-style SQL. It uses a VALUES fixture and common table expressions to keep the example self-contained. No claim is made that this was executed in a live database; the expected violating groups are worked through from the rows above.

codeExamples.code:
WITH order_lines (
    order_id,
    line_no,
    order_date,
    customer_id,
    customer_name,
    customer_tier,
    product_id,
    product_name,
    category,
    category_manager,
    quantity
) AS (
    VALUES
    (1001, 1, DATE '2026-01-10', 'C001', 'Ada Lim',  'Silver', 'P10', 'Trail Helmet', 'Safety',      'Lee',  1),
    (1001, 2, DATE '2026-01-10', 'C001', 'Ada Lim',  'Silver', 'P11', 'Bike Light',   'Safety',      'Lee',  2),
    (1002, 1, DATE '2026-01-11', 'C002', 'Bo Chen',  'Bronze', 'P12', 'Water Bottle', 'Accessories', 'Nora', 1),
    (1003, 1, DATE '2026-02-05', 'C001', 'Ada Lim',  'Gold',   'P13', 'Floor Pump',   'Accessories', 'Nora', 1),
    (1004, 1, DATE '2026-02-08', 'C003', 'Cy Diaz',  'Silver', 'P11', 'Bike Light',   'Safety',      'Noor', 1),
    (1004, 2, DATE '2026-02-08', 'C003', 'Cy Diaz',  'Silver', 'P14', 'Gloves',       'Apparel',     'Mina', 1),
    (1005, 1, DATE '2026-02-09', 'C002', 'Bo Chen',  'Bronze', 'P12', 'Water Bottle', 'Accessories', 'Nora', 2),
    (1006, 1, DATE '2026-02-12', 'C004', 'Dee Park', 'Bronze', 'P15', 'Energy Bar',   'Accessories', 'Mina', 5)
),
violations AS (
    SELECT
        'customer_id -> customer_tier' AS dependency,
        customer_id AS determinant,
        COUNT(DISTINCT customer_tier) AS distinct_dependent_values,
        STRING_AGG(DISTINCT customer_tier, ', ' ORDER BY customer_tier) AS observed_values
    FROM order_lines
    GROUP BY customer_id
    HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT customer_tier) > 1

    UNION ALL

    SELECT
        'category -> category_manager' AS dependency,
        category AS determinant,
        COUNT(DISTINCT category_manager) AS distinct_dependent_values,
        STRING_AGG(DISTINCT category_manager, ', ' ORDER BY category_manager) AS observed_values
    FROM order_lines
    GROUP BY category
    HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT category_manager) > 1

    UNION ALL

    SELECT
        'order_id -> product_id' AS dependency,
        CAST(order_id AS text) AS determinant,
        COUNT(DISTINCT product_id) AS distinct_dependent_values,
        STRING_AGG(DISTINCT product_id, ', ' ORDER BY product_id) AS observed_values
    FROM order_lines
    GROUP BY order_id
    HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT product_id) > 1
)
SELECT *
FROM violations
ORDER BY dependency, determinant;

sections.heading: Working through the results
paragraphs: The expected counterexamples are easy to verify from the fixture. For customer_id -> customer_tier, customer C001 appears as Silver on order 1001 and Gold on order 1003. The dependency is violated because the same customer_id has two tier values. That does not automatically mean the data is wrong. It means customer_tier is not a stable customer-grain attribute in this dataset. It is likely a time-dependent customer attribute or an order-time snapshot.

The modeling response depends on the business meaning. If reports need the tier at the time of sale, then customer_tier belongs with an order-effective context, such as customer_id plus order_date or customer_id plus a tier effective-period table. If reports need the current tier, then storing historical row-level copies in the order-line table can mislead analysts because old order lines will retain old values unless intentionally restated.

For category -> category_manager, the fixture has Safety managed by Lee and Noor, and Accessories managed by Nora and Mina. The same category has multiple managers. Again, the violation is a clue, not a verdict. Category_manager may depend on category plus date, category plus region, category plus subcategory, or an organizational assignment table. If the table presents category_manager as if category alone determines it, rollups by manager can double count or shift responsibility in confusing ways.

The third proposed dependency, order_id -> product_id, also violates: order 1001 contains P10 and P11, and order 1004 contains P11 and P14. This is a useful counterexample because it is not a defect. It shows that order_id is a header-level determinant, while product_id lives at order-line grain. The violation tells you that order_id alone is not the grain of this table. If someone builds an order-level mart from this table and carries product_id along without aggregation rules, they are mixing grains.

Notice the difference between a helpful dependency and a bad one. customer_id -> customer_tier was plausible but failed, revealing a time-varying attribute. category -> category_manager was plausible but failed, revealing a missing assignment context. order_id -> product_id failed because the proposed dependency contradicted the stated order-line grain. All three results teach something, but only the first two are likely wrong-grain attribute candidates.

sections.heading: Turn violations into modeling decisions
paragraphs: A dependency check should end in a modeling decision, not just a test failure. For each violation, ask three questions: what did we assume the determinant was, what determinant does the data suggest instead, and what should analysts be allowed to infer from this column?

For customer_tier, a better model might separate current customer attributes from historical order attributes. A customer dimension can hold the current tier if reports intentionally use current-state grouping. A customer-tier history table can hold effective dates if reports need point-in-time behavior. An order fact or order header can store tier_at_order if the business wants the exact value captured when the order was placed.

For category_manager, a better model might introduce a category_manager_assignment table with effective dates. The order-line table could keep category and join through order_date when manager-at-sale is needed. If manager responsibility is not historically meaningful, the manager should not be stored as a line-level fact attribute; it should be looked up from the current organizational structure.

For order_id -> product_id, the fix is different. There may be nothing to fix in the source table. The issue appears when the table is consumed at order grain. If a downstream table has one row per order, it must aggregate line-level attributes or omit them. For example, total_quantity can be summed, but product_id cannot be selected as a single value unless the table is filtered to one-line orders or a rule such as primary_product_id is explicitly defined.

sections.heading: A practical checklist
paragraphs: Use dependency checks as lightweight model reviews during development, not only as production tests. They are especially useful when a wide analytical table has been assembled from facts, dimensions, and snapshots, because wide tables can hide grain mismatches behind convenient column names.

The workflow is simple. First, write down the declared grain in one sentence. Second, list attributes that look like they belong to a coarser or different grain. Third, propose dependencies in plain language. Fourth, run grouped distinct-count checks. Fifth, interpret each violation with the business meaning before changing the model.

Be careful with nulls. Depending on the SQL engine and expression used, COUNT(DISTINCT column) may ignore null values. If null versus non-null is meaningful, handle nulls explicitly in the diagnostic. Also be careful with descriptive text fields such as names. A dependency violation on customer_name may be a spelling cleanup issue rather than a grain issue. The diagnostic finds counterexamples; the modeler still decides what those counterexamples mean.
bullets: If a dependent attribute changes for the same determinant, it probably has a finer grain, a time component, or a missing business qualifier.
If a proposed dependency fails because the determinant is too coarse, do not force the data to comply; restate the grain or choose the correct determinant.
If a downstream table changes grain, line-level descriptors need aggregation, exclusion, or an explicit selection rule.

takeaways: Functional dependency violations are practical counterexamples to grain assumptions in analytical tables.
A violation does not automatically prove bad data; it shows that the dependent attribute is not determined by the columns you thought determined it.
Wrong-grain fixes usually involve adding time context, moving the attribute to a dimension or assignment table, or removing the attribute from a coarser-grain output.

title: Composite keys in business event data
description: A practical guide to deciding when several columns together identify one business event, using a hypothetical retail event fixture with counterexamples and diagnostic SQL.
primaryKeyword: Composite keys in business event data
relatedKeywords: Composite keys in business event data
lead: A composite key is not just a group of columns that happens to be unique today. In business event data, the useful question is narrower: which columns together identify one occurrence of the event at the grain your table claims to store? This article works through that decision with a small hypothetical retail dataset and several counterexamples.

sections.heading: Start with the event grain
paragraphs: Before choosing a key, write the event grain in one sentence. For example: one row represents one item line recorded on a point-of-sale receipt. That sentence is doing more work than the column list. It says the row is not one customer visit, not one receipt, not one SKU per day, and not one final order total. It is one item line event.

A composite key is appropriate when no single available column identifies that event, but a minimal set of columns does. In relational terms, a candidate key is a set of attributes that uniquely identifies a tuple, and a composite candidate key uses more than one attribute. Minimality matters: if removing a column still leaves the rows uniquely identified under the business rule, the larger set is not the key; it is a superkey.

For event data, this decision depends on the source system’s numbering rules and the event’s business scope. Receipt numbers may reset each day. Line numbers may only be meaningful within a receipt. Register identifiers may only be unique within a store. Customer identifiers usually identify people or accounts, not event occurrences. A column can be useful context without being part of the event identity.

This article is not a general argument for or against surrogate keys. A warehouse may add a generated event_id for storage, joins, or ingestion mechanics. That does not remove the modeling question. If the business event is naturally identified by store_id, register_id, business_date, receipt_no, and line_no, then those columns still describe the event’s alternate key even when a surrogate is present.
bullets: Declare the row grain before evaluating uniqueness.
Use business rules about numbering scope, not only distinct counts in one extract.
Require the key to be minimal: every column must be necessary.
Separate event identity from descriptive attributes such as customer_id, sku, or amount.

sections.heading: A hypothetical retail fixture with counterexamples
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical retailer that records item lines from store registers. The source system assigns receipt numbers per register per business day. Within each receipt, line_no identifies the item line printed on the receipt. The proposed event table is pos_item_event, and the intended grain is one item line on one receipt.

The following fixture is deliberately small. It includes rows that break tempting but wrong keys. The expected composite key for the stated assumptions is store_id, register_id, business_date, receipt_no, line_no.

Rows 1 and 2 show that receipt_no alone is too broad because a receipt has multiple item lines. Rows 1 and 3 show that receipt_no plus line_no is still too broad because another store can issue the same receipt and line number. Rows 1 and 4 show that business_date is needed when receipt numbers reset on later days. Rows 1 and 5 show that register_id is needed when registers in the same store can issue overlapping receipt numbers. Rows 6 and 7 show that sku is not a safe substitute for line_no because the same SKU can appear twice on the same receipt as separate item lines.

Under the stated assumptions, the five-column combination identifies each row in the fixture. More importantly, each column has a reason to be present. store_id scopes the register. register_id scopes the receipt sequence. business_date handles the daily reset. receipt_no identifies the receipt within that register and date. line_no identifies the item line within the receipt.

The fixture also shows why sample uniqueness is not enough. In a quiet store, receipt_no and line_no may appear unique for a day’s extract. That does not make them an event key if the source rules allow the same pair tomorrow, in another store, or at another register.

sections.heading: Test candidates against counterexamples, not just counts
paragraphs: A practical key review starts by proposing candidate sets and asking what real or plausible case would violate each one. The goal is not to make every possible combination unique. The goal is to find the minimal set that identifies the event under the declared grain and source rules.

For the hypothetical POS event, receipt_no is rejected because receipts have multiple lines and receipt numbers repeat. receipt_no plus line_no is rejected because that pair is only meaningful within a broader issuing context. store_id, business_date, receipt_no, and line_no is tempting, but it is rejected if registers issue receipt numbers independently inside the same store. store_id, register_id, business_date, receipt_no, and sku is rejected because the same SKU can be scanned twice on the same receipt. customer_id, business_date, and sku is rejected because a customer can buy the same SKU more than once in a day, and because customer_id does not identify the register transaction.

The diagnostic SQL below is illustrative PostgreSQL-style SQL, not execution evidence. It checks whether a proposed key has duplicate groups in a loaded table. A duplicate result means the proposed key cannot identify one row at the declared grain. A zero-row result is not a proof by itself; it only says the loaded data did not contradict the candidate. You still need the source rules and counterexamples.

After a candidate passes the duplicate check, test minimality by removing one column at a time. If removing register_id still produces no duplicates in a small sample, do not immediately drop it. Ask whether the source rules guarantee receipt numbers are unique across all registers in a store for a business day. If they do not, register_id remains part of the key even if this extract happens not to expose the collision.
bullets: A duplicate group disproves a candidate key for the loaded data.
No duplicates in one sample do not prove the business rule.
A key column is justified by the event’s numbering scope, not by habit.
Minimality is tested against rules and plausible counterexamples, not only against today’s file.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative PostgreSQL-style diagnostic: find duplicate groups for the proposed key.
select
  store_id,
  register_id,
  business_date,
  receipt_no,
  line_no,
  count(*) as row_count
from pos_item_event
group by
  store_id,
  register_id,
  business_date,
  receipt_no,
  line_no
having count(*) > 1;

-- Counterexample check: show why receipt_no plus line_no is not enough.
select
  receipt_no,
  line_no,
  count(*) as row_count
from pos_item_event
group by receipt_no, line_no
having count(*) > 1;

-- Minimality probe: if this returns duplicates, register_id is necessary in the loaded data.
select
  store_id,
  business_date,
  receipt_no,
  line_no,
  count(*) as row_count
from pos_item_event
group by
  store_id,
  business_date,
  receipt_no,
  line_no
having count(*) > 1;

sections.heading: When the composite key needs another column
paragraphs: Sometimes the five-column POS key above is still not enough, because the event grain was misstated. Suppose the table stores every register action, including sale, void, return, and price override actions. Now one receipt line may have multiple events over time. If the row is one register action, line_no identifies the line affected, not the action itself. The key may need event_type plus action_sequence, source_event_no, or an event timestamp if the source guarantees it is unique at the required scope.

This is a grain problem, not a performance problem. Adding more columns to force uniqueness can hide the fact that the table mixes different event types. If sale rows and void rows are both present, decide whether the table is a line-item state table or an event log. A line-item state table might have one row per current receipt line and include status. An event log might have one row per action and use a different key. Both designs can be valid, but they answer different questions.

Another common change occurs when events are consolidated from several source systems. If two POS platforms both use store_id, register_id, business_date, receipt_no, and line_no, those values may collide after integration. In that case, source_system or source_instance can be part of the composite key, or the ingestion process can map each source event to a durable enterprise event identifier. The modeling rule is the same: the key must identify one event within the universe of rows stored in the table.

Do not add mutable descriptive attributes just to break ties. Amount, product name, cashier name, customer segment, and loyalty status are usually facts about the event or related entities, not identifiers of the event. If changing a value would create a new key for what the business still considers the same event, the column probably does not belong in the event key.
bullets: If one receipt line can have multiple actions, line_no may identify the line but not the event.
If multiple source systems are merged, include the source scope or map to a shared event identifier.
Avoid using mutable descriptions to make a weak key look unique.
A wider key is acceptable only when each added column narrows the event’s identity.

sections.heading: Enforce and document the decision
paragraphs: Once the key is chosen, write it down near the model definition: one row per item line recorded on a POS receipt; identified by store_id, register_id, business_date, receipt_no, and line_no. Also document the assumptions that make it true: receipt numbers are assigned per register per business day, line numbers are unique within a receipt, and the table stores item line records rather than every register action.

Relational databases commonly support primary key and unique constraints over multiple columns. In an analytical warehouse, the same idea may appear as a model test rather than a physical constraint. The important part is that the rule is executable somewhere. If duplicates appear, the failure should tell the data team whether the grain is wrong, the source assumptions changed, or the ingestion process duplicated an event.

A generated event_id can still be useful. It can make downstream joins shorter and insulate consumers from a long natural identifier. But the generated value should not be the only recorded answer to the identity question. Keeping the composite key as an enforced or tested alternate key preserves the business rule and makes duplicate diagnosis possible.

A good composite key decision leaves a clear audit trail: this is the event, this is its scope, these are the columns that identify it, these are the counterexamples that rejected smaller candidates, and these are the tests or constraints that guard the rule.
bullets: Document the grain and the key together.
Preserve the business key even if a surrogate event_id is added.
Turn the key rule into a constraint, model test, or duplicate diagnostic.
Revisit the key when the table’s event universe expands.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative PostgreSQL-style constraint for the hypothetical table.
-- This is a modeling example, not a recommendation about physical tuning.
alter table pos_item_event
add constraint pos_item_event_business_key
unique (store_id, register_id, business_date, receipt_no, line_no);

takeaways: A composite key is justified when multiple columns are jointly necessary to identify one event at the declared grain.
Counterexamples are the fastest way to reject attractive but wrong keys, such as receipt_no plus line_no when numbers repeat by store, register, or date.
Sample uniqueness is not enough. Use source numbering rules, plausible collisions, and minimality checks before accepting a composite key.
Generated surrogate identifiers can coexist with composite business keys, but they should not erase the documented event identity rule.

title: Natural keys versus surrogate keys
description: A practical guide to explaining identifier stability when a source customer identifier changes, using a small hypothetical retail dataset and counterexamples.
lead: The practical question in natural keys versus surrogate keys is not whether business identifiers are good or bad. It is whether the identifier you choose will continue to identify the same thing after source systems rename, merge, split, or reissue values. This guide uses a small hypothetical retail example to show why a changing source customer ID is usually a poor primary identifier for analytical relationships, and how to model the stable identity without throwing away the source identifier.

sections.heading: The stability question behind the key debate
paragraphs: A natural key is an identifier made from attributes that come from the business domain, such as a loyalty number, product SKU, tax ID, or source customer ID. A surrogate key is an identifier assigned by the data model or database, such as customer_key 501. In practice, the important distinction is not whether the value looks meaningful. The important question is whether the value is stable for the entity you are trying to identify.

Assume the prerequisite idea of candidate keys: a candidate key must uniquely identify one row at the intended grain. For a customer dimension, the grain might be one real-world customer identity. For an order fact, the grain might be one order event. A value can be unique today and still fail as a long-term identifier if it can change for the same entity or be reused for a different entity.

A source customer ID is especially tempting because it often arrives already populated, already indexed in the source application, and already present on events. But a source ID is usually a source-system identifier, not necessarily an enterprise identity. It may be stable inside one application while still changing when accounts migrate regions, when a CRM is replaced, when duplicate profiles are merged, or when guest accounts convert to loyalty accounts.
bullets: Ask: does this value identify the business entity, or only the source system’s current row for that entity?
Ask: can the value change while the entity remains the same?
Ask: can the value be reused after deletion, migration, or account closure?
Ask: does the value exist at the time every dependent fact is created?

sections.heading: A hypothetical retail fixture where the source ID changes
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical retail dataset with customers and orders. The source application emits a source_customer_id on every customer profile and order. At first glance, source_customer_id looks like a natural key for the customer table because it is populated and unique in each daily feed.

On 2026-01-10, the source has customer C-100 with loyalty number L-9001 and email ana@example.test. That customer places order O-1 for 100. On 2026-01-20, the same source ID C-100 places order O-2 for 50. On 2026-02-01, the retailer migrates customers in one region to a new account namespace. The same real-world loyalty member now appears as source customer E-778, still associated with loyalty number L-9001. On 2026-02-05, E-778 places order O-3 for 40.

There is also a second customer, C-200, with loyalty number L-9002, who places order O-4 for 20. The correct customer-level revenue is straightforward: the customer behind L-9001 has 100 + 50 + 40 = 190, and the customer behind L-9002 has 20. The modeling problem is that this correct result is not recoverable if the changing source ID is treated as the stable customer identity without an alias history.
This is a hypothetical example, not a claim about a specific retailer or source system. The numbers are deliberately small so the expected result can be checked by inspection.
bullets: C-100 and E-778 are two source identifiers for the same customer identity.
The business event amounts are 100, 50, 40, and 20.
The correct total for the first customer identity is 190, not 150 or 40.
The model needs to preserve the source identifiers while relating both to a stable customer identity.

sections.heading: Counterexample: using the changing source ID as the customer identity
paragraphs: If source_customer_id is used as the primary customer identifier in the analytical model, orders before and after the migration are split into different customer groups. The source ID remains useful for lineage and reconciliation, but it does not provide the stable identity needed for customer-level analysis.

The following illustrative SQL encodes the counterexample. It is not a benchmark and does not rely on engine-specific performance behavior. The expected grouped result is C-100 = 150, C-200 = 20, and E-778 = 40, which is wrong for the customer identity question because C-100 and E-778 represent the same customer.

codeExamples.code:
WITH orders(order_id, source_customer_id, order_date, amount) AS (
  VALUES
    ('O-1', 'C-100', DATE '2026-01-10', 100.00),
    ('O-2', 'C-100', DATE '2026-01-20',  50.00),
    ('O-3', 'E-778', DATE '2026-02-05',  40.00),
    ('O-4', 'C-200', DATE '2026-02-05',  20.00)
)
SELECT
  source_customer_id,
  SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY source_customer_id
ORDER BY source_customer_id;

sections.heading: Why simply updating the natural key does not fix the history
paragraphs: One reaction is to update C-100 to E-778 everywhere. That can make the current customer table look tidy, but it destroys part of the historical evidence unless the old identifier is retained somewhere. Historical events arrived with C-100. Reconciliation to the source feed, audit questions, and late-arriving events may still need to know that C-100 was a valid source identifier for the customer at the time.

Another reaction is to make source_customer_id a mutable primary key and let updates cascade to related tables. That treats a business correction as though it were the same as an identifier correction. Sometimes a source really did send the wrong ID and a correction should be applied. But a namespace migration is different: C-100 was not wrong on 2026-01-10. It was the identifier that the source used at that time.

A relational model should be able to say both things at once: the stable customer identity is the same across the migration, and the observed source identifiers changed over time. A single mutable natural key is a poor place to store both claims.
bullets: Do not overwrite away old source identifiers if they are needed for lineage, reconciliation, or late events.
Do not assume every source ID change means the previous value was erroneous.
Do not confuse the source row’s current identifier with the analytical entity’s durable identity.

sections.heading: Model the stable identity explicitly
paragraphs: A more robust design separates the stable customer identity from the source identifiers that have represented it. The customer table gets a surrogate customer_key that identifies the analytical customer identity. A separate identity map records which source identifiers map to that customer_key and when they were valid. Facts can then join through the map, preserving both stable analysis and source traceability.

In the hypothetical fixture, customer_key 501 represents the customer who was C-100 before 2026-02-01 and E-778 starting on 2026-02-01. Customer_key 502 represents C-200. When orders join through the identity map using both the source ID and the event date, the revenue rolls up to the stable customer identity: customer_key 501 has 190, and customer_key 502 has 20.

This does not mean the surrogate key magically solves identity resolution. The model still needs business rules for deciding that C-100 and E-778 are the same customer. In this example, the rule uses the stable loyalty number L-9001. In another dataset, the rule might require a merge table from the source, a customer master record, or a reviewed identity-resolution process. The surrogate key gives the model a stable place to attach that decision.

codeExamples.code:
WITH identity_map(source_customer_id, customer_key, valid_from, valid_to) AS (
  VALUES
    ('C-100', 501, DATE '2026-01-01', DATE '2026-02-01'),
    ('E-778', 501, DATE '2026-02-01', NULL),
    ('C-200', 502, DATE '2026-01-01', NULL)
),
orders(order_id, source_customer_id, order_date, amount) AS (
  VALUES
    ('O-1', 'C-100', DATE '2026-01-10', 100.00),
    ('O-2', 'C-100', DATE '2026-01-20',  50.00),
    ('O-3', 'E-778', DATE '2026-02-05',  40.00),
    ('O-4', 'C-200', DATE '2026-02-05',  20.00)
)
SELECT
  m.customer_key,
  SUM(o.amount) AS revenue
FROM orders o
JOIN identity_map m
  ON o.source_customer_id = m.source_customer_id
 AND o.order_date >= m.valid_from
 AND (m.valid_to IS NULL OR o.order_date < m.valid_to)
GROUP BY m.customer_key
ORDER BY m.customer_key;

sections.heading: Where natural keys still belong
paragraphs: The lesson is not that natural keys are always wrong. A natural key can be appropriate when the business truly controls its stability at the modeled grain, when changes are rare and explicitly governed, and when downstream relationships can tolerate the key’s shape and meaning. A country code reference table, a controlled internal product code, or a ledger account number may be reasonable natural-key candidates in the right organization.

But a natural key should earn that role. It should be evaluated as a candidate key, not accepted because it arrived from a source feed. If the key can change for the same entity, then using it as the primary relationship target will split history unless the model has a durable identity above it. If the key can be reused for a different entity, then it can create false joins across time. If the key can be absent, then it cannot identify every row at the intended grain.

In dimensional modeling language, Kimball distinguishes natural keys from more durable or surrogate identifiers, and describes surrogate keys as a common technique for dimension rows. The important practical point for this article is narrower: keep the source natural key as data, but do not force it to carry a stability promise it cannot keep.
bullets: Use natural keys when they are genuinely stable, unique, and mandatory at the modeled grain.
Use surrogate keys when the model needs a stable internal identifier independent of changing source values.
Keep source natural keys as alternate keys or lineage attributes even when they are not the primary analytical identity.

sections.heading: Constraints and diagnostics that make the decision concrete
paragraphs: Surrogate keys do not remove the need for constraints. They create a stable target for relationships, but the model still needs rules that prevent ambiguous mappings. Relational constraints such as primary keys, unique constraints, and foreign keys express these rules in the schema when the database supports and enforces them. PostgreSQL’s documentation, for example, describes these constraint types as mechanisms for maintaining data integrity; the same modeling ideas apply beyond one engine even though syntax and enforcement details vary.

For the hypothetical identity map, useful checks include: no duplicate active mapping for the same source system and source customer ID at the same time; no overlapping validity windows for the same source identifier; every order should map to exactly one customer_key for its event date; and every customer_key should be traceable to the business rule or source record that created it. Some of these checks can be enforced with database constraints. Others may need data tests because temporal non-overlap rules are more complex than a single-column unique constraint.

A good diagnostic query for this topic is not only “are source_customer_id values unique today?” It is “has any supposedly stable identifier mapped to multiple customer identities, or has one customer identity been represented by multiple source identifiers over time?” The first case warns about false merges. The second case warns that using the source ID alone will split history.
bullets: Test uniqueness at the grain and time period you actually use.
Track identifier changes as first-class data, not as accidental updates.
Require facts to map to exactly one stable identity when the metric depends on that identity.
Investigate both false splits and false merges; either can make customer metrics wrong.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative diagnostic: source IDs that appear under more than one stable identity.
SELECT
  source_system,
  source_customer_id,
  COUNT(DISTINCT customer_key) AS customer_identity_count
FROM customer_identity_map
GROUP BY source_system, source_customer_id
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT customer_key) > 1;

-- Illustrative diagnostic: customer identities represented by multiple source IDs.
SELECT
  customer_key,
  COUNT(DISTINCT source_customer_id) AS source_id_count
FROM customer_identity_map
GROUP BY customer_key
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT source_customer_id) > 1;

sections.heading: A decision rule for practitioners
paragraphs: When explaining natural keys versus surrogate keys to a team, avoid framing it as a matter of taste. Frame it as a stability contract. The primary key used by other tables is a promise that the same value will continue to identify the same entity at the chosen grain. If the business cannot make that promise for a source identifier, the analytical model should not pretend otherwise.

For the hypothetical retail case, source_customer_id is still valuable. It should be stored, indexed where useful, and used for reconciliation to the source. It may participate in an alternate key with source_system and valid dates. But it should not be the stable customer identity because the example shows a same-customer ID change that would split revenue from 190 into 150 and 40.

The concise rule is: use the natural key when it is stable enough to be the relationship target; use a surrogate key when the model needs a stable identity that can survive changes in source identifiers; and keep the natural identifiers as governed attributes so the model remains explainable.

takeaways: The real issue in natural keys versus surrogate keys is identifier stability at the modeled grain, not whether the value is human-readable.
A changing source customer ID can be unique in each feed and still be wrong as the stable customer identity because it splits history.
A surrogate customer_key plus an identity map preserves both stable analysis and source traceability, but it still requires explicit business rules and data quality checks.
Natural keys remain useful as alternate keys, lineage attributes, and reconciliation handles even when they should not be primary relationship targets.

title: Referential integrity across analytical tables
description: A practical guide to detecting orphaned facts in analytical tables while preserving legitimate late-arriving dimensions and pending dimension matches.
lead: Analytical warehouses often cannot treat referential integrity exactly like an OLTP database. A fact row can arrive before its dimension row is complete, but that does not mean every missing dimension reference is acceptable. The useful practice is to classify missing references: preserve legitimate late-arriving dimensions, isolate real orphans, and make the unresolved middle visible.

sections.heading: Why analytical referential integrity is different
paragraphs: In a transactional system, a foreign key from an order to a customer can often be enforced at write time. If the customer does not exist, the transaction is rejected. Analytical tables have a different timing problem. Facts, dimensions, and corrections may arrive from different source feeds, at different times, and with different levels of completeness.

The relational expectation still matters: an order fact that claims to belong to customer key 101 should have a corresponding customer dimension row for key 101. Without that expectation, joins become ambiguous, measures disappear under inner joins, and analysts cannot tell whether missing attributes mean “unknown,” “not yet loaded,” or “bad reference.”

The trap is treating every non-match as the same defect. Kimball dimensional modeling guidance distinguishes late-arriving dimensions and late-arriving facts. A fact can arrive before all dimension attributes are known, and a dimension can be inferred first and completed later. That means the data engineering check should not simply delete, reject, or inner join away every fact that does not currently have a fully populated dimension row.

A better rule is: detect orphaned facts without discarding legitimate late dimensions. The check needs to separate at least five cases: a normal match, a match to an inferred late-arriving dimension row, a recent fact still inside an accepted dimension-arrival window, an aged missing dimension, and a populated foreign key that points nowhere.

sections.heading: A hypothetical retail fixture with counterexamples
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical retail order mart. The fact table records one row per order. The customer dimension has a warehouse customer key and a source customer identifier. The source identifier is included only to help diagnose arrival timing; the example does not depend on a broader debate about natural and surrogate keys.

The dimension includes an agreed unknown customer row with key 0. It also includes one inferred customer row: customer key 102 exists because an order arrived before the customer profile was complete. That row is not an orphan; it is a deliberate placeholder that should be completed later.

Assume the diagnostic runs at 2026-02-16 00:00:00 and the team allows a two-day grace period for customer dimensions to arrive. A fact loaded on or after 2026-02-14 00:00:00 with no customer key is still pending. A fact older than that with no customer key has exceeded the grace period. These thresholds are business rules, not universal constants.
bullets: Order O1002 is a legitimate late-arriving dimension case because it joins to an inferred customer dimension row.
Order O1003 is not yet an orphan because it was loaded inside the two-day grace period and still carries a source customer id.
Order O1004 is an orphaned surrogate-key reference because it points to customer key 999, which is absent from the customer dimension.
Order O1006 is an aged missing dimension because it has no customer key and has exceeded the grace period.
Order O1007 is routed to the explicit unknown customer member, which is different from an accidental non-match.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative SQL fixture. Syntax may need minor adaptation by engine.
WITH dim_customer AS (
    SELECT 0 AS customer_key, 'UNKNOWN' AS source_customer_id, 'Unknown customer' AS customer_name, FALSE AS is_inferred
    UNION ALL SELECT 101, 'C001', 'Aster Bikes', FALSE
    UNION ALL SELECT 102, 'C002', 'Inferred pending profile', TRUE
    UNION ALL SELECT 103, 'C003', 'Northwind Outlet', FALSE
),
fact_order AS (
    SELECT 'O1001' AS order_id, DATE '2026-02-10' AS order_date, 'C001' AS source_customer_id, 101 AS customer_key, 120.00 AS order_amount, TIMESTAMP '2026-02-10 09:10:00' AS load_received_at
    UNION ALL SELECT 'O1002', DATE '2026-02-11', 'C002', 102, 45.00, TIMESTAMP '2026-02-11 10:00:00'
    UNION ALL SELECT 'O1003', DATE '2026-02-15', 'C004', NULL, 80.00, TIMESTAMP '2026-02-15 08:30:00'
    UNION ALL SELECT 'O1004', DATE '2026-02-13', 'C999', 999, 22.00, TIMESTAMP '2026-02-10 07:45:00'
    UNION ALL SELECT 'O1005', DATE '2026-02-14', 'C003', 103, 60.00, TIMESTAMP '2026-02-14 12:00:00'
    UNION ALL SELECT 'O1006', DATE '2026-02-10', 'C005', NULL, 35.00, TIMESTAMP '2026-02-10 11:00:00'
    UNION ALL SELECT 'O1007', DATE '2026-02-12', NULL, 0, 15.00, TIMESTAMP '2026-02-12 14:00:00'
)
SELECT *
FROM fact_order;

sections.heading: Counterexample: an inner join hides the problem
paragraphs: A common mistake is to validate a fact table by joining it to the dimension and checking whether the query returns rows. An inner join is not a referential integrity diagnostic. It silently removes the evidence you need to inspect.

In the fixture, the total order amount is 377.00. An inner join from facts to customer dimension on customer_key returns O1001, O1002, O1005, and O1007. It drops O1003 because the customer key is not assigned yet, drops O1004 because key 999 does not exist, and drops O1006 because no key was assigned. The joined total is 240.00, not because the business only took 240.00 of orders, but because 137.00 was filtered out by the join.

That discarded 137.00 mixes different meanings: 80.00 is a recent pending late-dimension case, 22.00 is a bad populated key, and 35.00 is an aged unresolved dimension. The inner join removes all three and gives the team no way to decide what should happen next.

codeExamples.code:
WITH dim_customer AS (
    SELECT 0 AS customer_key, 'UNKNOWN' AS source_customer_id, 'Unknown customer' AS customer_name, FALSE AS is_inferred
    UNION ALL SELECT 101, 'C001', 'Aster Bikes', FALSE
    UNION ALL SELECT 102, 'C002', 'Inferred pending profile', TRUE
    UNION ALL SELECT 103, 'C003', 'Northwind Outlet', FALSE
),
fact_order AS (
    SELECT 'O1001' AS order_id, DATE '2026-02-10' AS order_date, 'C001' AS source_customer_id, 101 AS customer_key, 120.00 AS order_amount, TIMESTAMP '2026-02-10 09:10:00' AS load_received_at
    UNION ALL SELECT 'O1002', DATE '2026-02-11', 'C002', 102, 45.00, TIMESTAMP '2026-02-11 10:00:00'
    UNION ALL SELECT 'O1003', DATE '2026-02-15', 'C004', NULL, 80.00, TIMESTAMP '2026-02-15 08:30:00'
    UNION ALL SELECT 'O1004', DATE '2026-02-13', 'C999', 999, 22.00, TIMESTAMP '2026-02-10 07:45:00'
    UNION ALL SELECT 'O1005', DATE '2026-02-14', 'C003', 103, 60.00, TIMESTAMP '2026-02-14 12:00:00'
    UNION ALL SELECT 'O1006', DATE '2026-02-10', 'C005', NULL, 35.00, TIMESTAMP '2026-02-10 11:00:00'
    UNION ALL SELECT 'O1007', DATE '2026-02-12', NULL, 0, 15.00, TIMESTAMP '2026-02-12 14:00:00'
)
SELECT
    COUNT(*) AS joined_order_count,
    SUM(f.order_amount) AS joined_order_amount
FROM fact_order f
JOIN dim_customer d
  ON f.customer_key = d.customer_key;

-- Expected result for this fixture:
-- joined_order_count = 4
-- joined_order_amount = 240.00

sections.heading: A classification query for orphan detection
paragraphs: Use a left join, but do not stop at “dimension row is null.” Add the timing and modeling rules that distinguish acceptable lateness from a true orphan. The output should be a classified exception set, not just a pass/fail result.

The order of the cases matters. A reserved unknown member is a modeled route and should not be confused with an accidental missing dimension row. A populated customer key that fails to join is usually more suspicious than a null customer key, because the fact claims a specific warehouse key that the dimension does not contain. An inferred dimension row is a successful reference, but it should remain visible because too many inferred rows can indicate upstream customer-profile latency.

For the hypothetical fixture, the expected classification is six categories: two matched real-dimension facts totaling 180.00, one inferred late-dimension match totaling 45.00, one recent pending late-dimension fact totaling 80.00, one orphaned surrogate-key fact totaling 22.00, one aged missing-dimension fact totaling 35.00, and one unknown-member route totaling 15.00. The immediately actionable referential defects are O1004 and O1006, totaling 57.00. O1002 and O1003 should not be discarded.

codeExamples.code:
WITH dim_customer AS (
    SELECT 0 AS customer_key, 'UNKNOWN' AS source_customer_id, 'Unknown customer' AS customer_name, FALSE AS is_inferred
    UNION ALL SELECT 101, 'C001', 'Aster Bikes', FALSE
    UNION ALL SELECT 102, 'C002', 'Inferred pending profile', TRUE
    UNION ALL SELECT 103, 'C003', 'Northwind Outlet', FALSE
),
fact_order AS (
    SELECT 'O1001' AS order_id, DATE '2026-02-10' AS order_date, 'C001' AS source_customer_id, 101 AS customer_key, 120.00 AS order_amount, TIMESTAMP '2026-02-10 09:10:00' AS load_received_at
    UNION ALL SELECT 'O1002', DATE '2026-02-11', 'C002', 102, 45.00, TIMESTAMP '2026-02-11 10:00:00'
    UNION ALL SELECT 'O1003', DATE '2026-02-15', 'C004', NULL, 80.00, TIMESTAMP '2026-02-15 08:30:00'
    UNION ALL SELECT 'O1004', DATE '2026-02-13', 'C999', 999, 22.00, TIMESTAMP '2026-02-10 07:45:00'
    UNION ALL SELECT 'O1005', DATE '2026-02-14', 'C003', 103, 60.00, TIMESTAMP '2026-02-14 12:00:00'
    UNION ALL SELECT 'O1006', DATE '2026-02-10', 'C005', NULL, 35.00, TIMESTAMP '2026-02-10 11:00:00'
    UNION ALL SELECT 'O1007', DATE '2026-02-12', NULL, 0, 15.00, TIMESTAMP '2026-02-12 14:00:00'
),
classified AS (
    SELECT
        f.order_id,
        f.source_customer_id,
        f.customer_key,
        f.order_amount,
        f.load_received_at,
        d.customer_name,
        d.is_inferred,
        CASE
            WHEN f.customer_key = 0 AND d.customer_key IS NOT NULL
                THEN 'unknown_member_route'
            WHEN f.customer_key IS NOT NULL AND d.customer_key IS NULL
                THEN 'orphaned_surrogate_key'
            WHEN d.customer_key IS NOT NULL AND d.is_inferred = TRUE
                THEN 'matched_inferred_late_dimension'
            WHEN f.customer_key IS NULL
                 AND d.customer_key IS NULL
                 AND f.load_received_at >= TIMESTAMP '2026-02-14 00:00:00'
                THEN 'pending_late_dimension_within_grace'
            WHEN f.customer_key IS NULL AND d.customer_key IS NULL
                THEN 'aged_missing_dimension'
            ELSE 'matched_real_dimension'
        END AS reference_status
    FROM fact_order f
    LEFT JOIN dim_customer d
      ON f.customer_key = d.customer_key
)
SELECT
    reference_status,
    COUNT(*) AS order_count,
    SUM(order_amount) AS order_amount
FROM classified
GROUP BY reference_status
ORDER BY reference_status;

-- Expected result for this fixture:
-- aged_missing_dimension: 1 order, 35.00
-- matched_inferred_late_dimension: 1 order, 45.00
-- matched_real_dimension: 2 orders, 180.00
-- orphaned_surrogate_key: 1 order, 22.00
-- pending_late_dimension_within_grace: 1 order, 80.00
-- unknown_member_route: 1 order, 15.00

sections.heading: Turn the classification into a data contract
paragraphs: The diagnostic becomes useful when each status has an owner and a consequence. Otherwise, the query is just a report of known messiness. The contract should say which statuses are allowed in published marts, which are allowed only temporarily, and which should block or quarantine rows before broad consumption.

A reasonable pattern is to publish matched real dimensions, matched inferred dimensions, and explicit unknown-member routes if the business accepts them. Recent pending late dimensions can remain in a staging or exception area until the dimension arrives or the grace period expires. Orphaned surrogate keys and aged missing dimensions should be treated as defects because the model no longer has a credible path from the fact to the dimension.

There is a tradeoff. If the grace period is too short, the pipeline will raise false alarms during normal source latency. If it is too long, real defects remain mixed with ordinary pending data. The right window depends on the source system’s expected arrival pattern and the reporting tolerance for incomplete dimensional attributes.

The same classification can support both row-level repair and aggregate monitoring. Row-level output tells an engineer which orders need investigation. Aggregates tell the team whether a recurring upstream issue is getting worse. For example, a rising count of inferred customer rows might mean the customer-profile feed is lagging behind the order feed, even though the fact rows are not technically orphaned.
bullets: Matched real dimension: publish normally.
Matched inferred late dimension: publish if inferred dimensions are part of the model, but monitor completion.
Pending late dimension within grace: keep visible and reprocess when the dimension arrives; do not classify as a defect yet.
Orphaned surrogate key: investigate immediately because the fact points to a dimension key that does not exist.
Aged missing dimension: investigate or route to an agreed unknown member according to business rules.
Unknown member route: publish only if the unknown member is an explicit modeling choice, not a silent default.

sections.heading: Practical implementation notes
paragraphs: This article focuses on relational semantics, not engine tuning. The core pattern is portable: preserve facts, left join to the dimension, classify the reference status, and aggregate exceptions by status. In a production pipeline, the same logic might live in a transformation model, a data quality test, an exception table, or a reconciliation dashboard.

The most important implementation detail is to keep the exception rows. A boolean test such as “all fact customer keys exist in dim_customer” is too blunt for analytical loading. Store order_id, source_customer_id, customer_key, load time, reference_status, and the diagnostic run time. Those columns make the difference between a failed check and a repairable queue.

Another practical detail is to avoid using only aggregate thresholds. A rule such as “less than 0.1 percent orphaned facts is acceptable” may be useful for alerting, but it should not replace row-level classification. One high-value orphan can matter more than many low-value rows, and a small defect can reveal a broken key assignment path.

Finally, do not use the diagnostic as an excuse to discard facts. Inner joins, delete-and-reload shortcuts, and broad filters can make quality metrics look cleaner while making the analytical dataset less truthful. The goal is to preserve the business event, identify its current reference status, and repair the relationship when the necessary dimension information becomes available.

takeaways: Referential integrity still matters in analytical models, even when load timing prevents strict transactional enforcement.
A missing dimension match is not always an orphan; inferred dimensions and recent pending facts are legitimate late-arriving cases when they are explicitly modeled.
Use classification, not an inner join, to separate matched facts, inferred late dimensions, pending late dimensions, orphaned keys, aged missing dimensions, and unknown-member routes.
The example’s actionable defects are the orphaned populated key and the aged missing dimension, totaling 57.00; the late-arriving cases should remain visible rather than being discarded.
