title: Set semantics versus bag semantics in SQL
description: A practical guide to showing why duplicate rows survive ordinary SQL queries, using a small hypothetical retail dataset and grain-based diagnostics.
primaryKeyword: Set semantics versus bag semantics in SQL
relatedKeywords: Set semantics versus bag semantics in SQL
lead: SQL looks relational, but ordinary SELECT queries do not behave like pure set operations. Unless a query asks for duplicate elimination, SQL preserves duplicate rows. That matters when a join, projection, or report appears to be “duplicating” data. Often the query is doing exactly what bag semantics say it should do.

sections.heading: The reader problem: the same-looking row appears twice
paragraphs: A common debugging moment in analytics engineering is seeing the same customer, product, or date repeated in a result and asking whether SQL made a mistake. The short answer is no: ordinary SQL query results use bag semantics, also called multiset semantics. A bag can contain two rows with the same values. A mathematical set cannot.

Relational theory is usually introduced with sets. In set semantics, a relation has no duplicate tuples. But SQL tables and query results can contain duplicate rows unless constraints or query operators prevent them. A primary key can prevent duplicate identifiers in a base table. A UNIQUE constraint can prevent duplicate values for selected columns. Neither of those constraints says that every SELECT result must be duplicate-free.

This distinction is not an engine tuning issue. It is a modeling and query semantics issue. The practical skill is to identify the grain of each intermediate result: what one row represents at that point in the query. If the grain is “one order line,” then seeing a customer repeated across multiple rows is expected. If the desired grain is “one customer,” the query must aggregate, filter, or deduplicate intentionally.

sections.heading: A small hypothetical retail fixture
paragraphs: Use this hypothetical retail dataset. It is deliberately small enough to reason about by inspection. The important assumption is that declared identifiers are unique at their natural grain: one row per customer, one row per order, and one row per order line within an order.
The fixture avoids null-specific behavior. Every foreign key value shown has a matching parent row. The goal is only to show why ordinary projection and joins preserve duplicate-looking rows.
bullets: customers has grain one row per customer.
orders has grain one row per order.
order_lines has grain one row per line item on an order.
A customer may place many orders, and an order may have many lines.

sections.heading: Projection in SQL is not set projection unless you ask
paragraphs: Start with the simplest counterexample: select only customer_id from orders. The orders table has three rows. Two of those rows belong to customer C1. In relational algebra under set semantics, projecting only customer_id would produce the set of customer identifiers: C1 and C2. Ordinary SQL does not do that. It returns one output row for each input order row, with only the requested column retained.

The expected result has three rows: C1, C1, and C2. The two C1 rows are not contradictory. They represent two different input orders after the order_id column has been removed from the output. Once order_id is no longer visible, two rows can have the same displayed values while still being the result of two distinct input rows.

Adding DISTINCT changes the operator. It asks SQL to eliminate duplicate rows across the selected columns. The expected distinct result has two rows: C1 and C2. That is useful when the question is “which customers have placed at least one order?” It is wrong if the question is “how many orders are represented?” because it discards multiplicity.

codeExamples.code:
-- Ordinary SQL projection: expected rows are C1, C1, C2.
SELECT customer_id
FROM orders
ORDER BY customer_id;

-- Explicit duplicate elimination: expected rows are C1, C2.
SELECT DISTINCT customer_id
FROM orders
ORDER BY customer_id;

sections.heading: Joins preserve every matching combination
paragraphs: Joins are the second place where bag semantics surprise people. A join does not produce one row per customer just because customers is part of the query. It produces rows according to the matches between the joined inputs. PostgreSQL’s table expression documentation describes joined tables in terms of rows formed from matching rows of the inputs; the same conceptual rule is enough for this example.

Join customers to orders. Customer C1 matches two orders, so C1 appears twice. Customer C2 matches one order, so C2 appears once. Nothing is duplicated accidentally; the result grain is one row per order with customer attributes attached.

Now join through order_lines. Order O10 has two lines, O11 has one line, and O12 has one line. The result grain becomes one row per order line with customer and order attributes attached. Ada appears three times because Ada has three order lines across two orders. Ben appears once because Ben has one order line. If the query selects only customer_name, the output may look like duplicate customer rows, but the hidden grain is still order line.
This is the main diagnostic move: do not ask first whether duplicates exist. Ask what the query’s row grain is. A repeated value is only an error if it violates the intended grain.

codeExamples.code:
-- Expected result grain: one row per order.
-- Ada appears for O10 and O11; Ben appears for O12.
SELECT c.customer_name, o.order_id
FROM customers AS c
JOIN orders AS o
  ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
ORDER BY c.customer_name, o.order_id;

-- Expected result grain: one row per order line.
-- Rows: Ada/O10/1, Ada/O10/2, Ada/O11/1, Ben/O12/1.
SELECT c.customer_name, l.order_id, l.line_no, l.sku, l.quantity
FROM customers AS c
JOIN orders AS o
  ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
JOIN order_lines AS l
  ON l.order_id = o.order_id
ORDER BY c.customer_name, l.order_id, l.line_no;

sections.heading: Counterexample: DISTINCT can hide the wrong problem
paragraphs: Suppose a report wants one row per customer with two metrics: number of orders and number of order lines. A tempting but unsafe reaction to repeated customer rows is to add DISTINCT to the final SELECT. That may make the display shorter, but it does not answer the metric question. It can also hide a many-to-many join path that inflated counts before the final projection.

A better pattern is to aggregate at the intended grain before joining result sets. For this fixture, count orders per customer from orders, count lines per customer by joining orders to order_lines, then join the two customer-grain summaries. The Kimball Group’s guidance on multipass SQL addresses a related dimensional modeling concern: avoid direct fact-to-fact joins when combining metrics at different grains; aggregate each fact stream to a common grain first.

The arithmetic is checkable by inspection. C1 has orders O10 and O11, so order_count is 2. C1 has lines O10-1, O10-2, and O11-1, so line_count is 3. C2 has order O12 and line O12-1, so both counts are 1. The final customer-grain result should therefore be C1: 2 orders and 3 lines; C2: 1 order and 1 line.

codeExamples.code:
-- Customer-grain metrics by aggregating before the final join.
WITH order_counts AS (
  SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY customer_id
),
line_counts AS (
  SELECT o.customer_id, COUNT(*) AS line_count
  FROM orders AS o
  JOIN order_lines AS l
    ON l.order_id = o.order_id
  GROUP BY o.customer_id
)
SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.customer_name,
       oc.order_count,
       lc.line_count
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN order_counts AS oc
  ON oc.customer_id = c.customer_id
LEFT JOIN line_counts AS lc
  ON lc.customer_id = c.customer_id
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

-- Expected rows from the hypothetical fixture:
-- C1, Ada, 2, 3
-- C2, Ben, 1, 1

sections.heading: A diagnostic for duplicate-looking rows
paragraphs: When a result has duplicate-looking rows, compare the displayed row count with the count at the intended key. This is a semantics diagnostic, not a performance prescription. It helps separate three cases: expected multiplicity, missing key columns in the SELECT list, and a genuinely unintended join path.

For the order-line join above, the physical result has four rows. If the intended grain is customer, the same result contains only two distinct customer_ids. That mismatch is not automatically a bug, but it proves that the current query is not customer-grain. If the intended grain is order line, then the key is order_id plus line_no, and the four rows are exactly right.

Constraints help make this reasoning reliable. A primary key on customers states that customer_id identifies one customer row. A primary key on order_lines states that order_id plus line_no identifies one line row. PostgreSQL’s constraint documentation describes primary keys and unique constraints as mechanisms for enforcing uniqueness. The key point for modeling is that uniqueness belongs to declared or inferred grains; it does not magically propagate to every projection of a query.
bullets: Name the intended grain in one sentence: one row per customer, order, order line, day, or other entity.
List the columns that identify that grain.
Count result rows and count distinct grain keys.
If result rows exceed distinct grain keys, inspect joins and projections before adding DISTINCT.
Use DISTINCT only when duplicate elimination is part of the question, not as a reflexive cleanup step.

codeExamples.code:
-- Diagnostic: compare result rows with customer-grain rows.
WITH result AS (
  SELECT c.customer_id, c.customer_name, l.order_id, l.line_no
  FROM customers AS c
  JOIN orders AS o
    ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
  JOIN order_lines AS l
    ON l.order_id = o.order_id
)
SELECT
  COUNT(*) AS result_rows,
  COUNT(*) - (
    SELECT COUNT(*)
    FROM (SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM result) AS distinct_customers
  ) AS rows_above_customer_grain
FROM result;

-- From the fixture, result_rows is 4 and rows_above_customer_grain is 2.
-- That says the result is not one row per customer.

sections.heading: The practical rule
paragraphs: In SQL, duplicate rows survive ordinary relational queries because SQL generally operates on bags. SELECT keeps one output row for each qualifying input row. Projection can remove the columns that made those rows distinguishable. Joins form rows for matching combinations. DISTINCT, GROUP BY, and properly chosen aggregation are explicit changes to that behavior.

This is why “the query duplicated my customers” is often an imprecise diagnosis. More precise language is: “the query is at order-line grain, but I selected customer columns,” or “the join path creates multiple matches per intended key,” or “I need a customer-grain aggregate before the final join.” That phrasing points to the fix without erasing meaningful multiplicity.

takeaways: Ordinary SQL uses bag semantics: duplicate-looking rows can survive projection and joins unless duplicate elimination is explicitly requested.
A repeated value is not necessarily a duplicate entity. Determine the row grain before deciding whether the result is wrong.
DISTINCT is correct when the question requires unique selected rows, but it can hide grain mistakes and inflated intermediate results.
Primary keys and unique constraints enforce uniqueness in base tables or declared column sets; they do not guarantee every query result is duplicate-free.
For mixed-grain metrics, aggregate each input to the intended common grain before joining the summaries.

title: First normal form and repeating groups
description: A practical guide to reshaping repeating attributes into child tables while preserving the parent key, using a small hypothetical retail-order example with counterexamples and diagnostics.
primaryKeyword: First normal form and repeating groups
relatedKeywords: First normal form and repeating groups
lead: Repeating attributes are easy to create and painful to query. A table with item_1_sku, item_2_sku, and item_3_sku looks convenient until a fourth item appears, an item needs its own status, or an analyst must count products across orders. First normal form is the point where you stop hiding a set of child facts inside one parent row. The practical move is not just to split columns out; it is to split them out while carrying the parent key and the child grain with them.

sections.heading: The modeling problem: repeated facts inside one row
paragraphs: First normal form is often summarized as removing repeating groups and storing values from atomic domains. For practitioners, the useful test is simpler: if the same kind of fact appears multiple times in one row, and the column names differ mainly by a suffix or position, you probably have a repeating group.

Consider this hypothetical retail-order extract. It is not a benchmark or production example; it is a small fixture for reasoning about keys and dependencies. The business event is an order. Each order can contain zero or more purchased products. A compact spreadsheet-style design might store the first three products directly on the order row.

This design appears to preserve the order, because every product column sits beside order_id. But the relationship is only implicit. The parent order is mixed with several child item occurrences. The table’s candidate key may be order_id, but order_id does not identify a single product occurrence. It identifies a row that may contain several product facts.
bullets: Parent grain: one row per order.
Hidden child grain: one product occurrence within an order.
Symptom: item_1_sku, item_2_sku, and item_3_sku are the same attribute repeated by position.
Risk: the design has no stable place for the fourth item, item-level status, item-level discount, or item-level return reason.

codeExamples.code:
-- Hypothetical denormalized order extract
-- The numbered columns are the repeating group.
CREATE TABLE order_extract_bad (
  order_id        INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  order_date      DATE NOT NULL,
  customer_id     INTEGER NOT NULL,
  item_1_sku      TEXT,
  item_1_qty      INTEGER,
  item_1_price    NUMERIC(10,2),
  item_2_sku      TEXT,
  item_2_qty      INTEGER,
  item_2_price    NUMERIC(10,2),
  item_3_sku      TEXT,
  item_3_qty      INTEGER,
  item_3_price    NUMERIC(10,2)
);

INSERT INTO order_extract_bad VALUES
  (1001, DATE '2026-10-01', 501, 'MUG-BLUE', 2, 8.00, 'TEA-EARL', 1, 12.50, NULL, NULL, NULL),
  (1002, DATE '2026-10-01', 502, 'MUG-BLUE', 1, 8.00, NULL, NULL, NULL, NULL, NULL, NULL),
  (1003, DATE '2026-10-02', 501, 'INFUSER', 1, 6.00, 'TEA-GRN', 2, 11.00, 'HONEY', 1, 5.50);

sections.heading: Counterexamples: two ways to split the columns incorrectly
paragraphs: The fix is not merely to make a taller table. The fix is to preserve the parent relationship and define the child key. Two common counterexamples show why.

The first counterexample is to create an item table without order_id. This produces a bag of item facts, but no fact states which order contained which item. The parent-child relationship has been discarded. You can count sku values, but you cannot reconstruct order 1001.

The second counterexample is to create a child table with order_id and sku only, treating those two columns as the key. That fails when the same product can appear twice on an order for different reasons. For example, a customer might buy one mug at full price and another as part of a later promotion in the same order, or a source system might record separate item rows because they came from different fulfillment locations. Whether that can happen is a business rule. The data model should not accidentally prohibit it unless the rule is explicit.

A safer child grain is one row per order line. The line is identified by the parent order_id plus a line_number assigned by the source or by the ingestion process according to a deterministic rule. Now the row has an address: order 1003, line 2. The sku is an attribute of that line, not the identifier of the relationship itself.
bullets: Bad split 1: store sku, quantity, and price in a separate table but omit order_id. The parent relationship is lost.
Bad split 2: use order_id plus sku as the key when the same sku can occur more than once per order.
Better split: use order_id plus a child discriminator such as line_number, then store sku, quantity, and price as attributes of that child row.

codeExamples.code:
-- Counterexample: this table has item facts but no parent order.
CREATE TABLE order_item_orphan_bad (
  sku        TEXT NOT NULL,
  quantity   INTEGER NOT NULL,
  unit_price NUMERIC(10,2) NOT NULL
);

-- Counterexample: this key may be too narrow if a sku can appear twice on one order.
CREATE TABLE order_item_key_too_narrow_bad (
  order_id   INTEGER NOT NULL,
  sku        TEXT NOT NULL,
  quantity   INTEGER NOT NULL,
  unit_price NUMERIC(10,2) NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, sku)
);

sections.heading: A 1NF reshape that keeps the parent-child relationship
paragraphs: A first-normal-form design separates the parent order facts from the repeating item facts. The order table keeps facts that occur once per order: order date and customer id. The order_line table keeps facts that occur once per product occurrence within an order: sku, quantity, and unit price. The foreign key from order_line.order_id to orders.order_id is the preserved parent relationship.

This is not just cleaner column naming. It changes what the keys can say. orders.order_id identifies one order. order_line.order_id plus order_line.line_number identifies one line on that order. The model can now represent one item, three items, or thirty items without altering the table definition. It can also attach future line-level facts, such as fulfillment_status or return_reason, without adding item_1_return_reason, item_2_return_reason, and so on.

Here is the same hypothetical data reshaped. The expected line counts are easy to verify from the fixture: order 1001 has two non-null item slots, order 1002 has one, and order 1003 has three, for six order_line rows total. The relationship is not lost because every child row carries order_id.
bullets: Parent table grain: one row per order.
Child table grain: one row per order line.
Parent key: order_id.
Child key: order_id plus line_number.
Relationship: order_line.order_id references orders.order_id.

codeExamples.code:
-- Hypothetical 1NF reshape.
CREATE TABLE orders (
  order_id    INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  order_date  DATE NOT NULL,
  customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE order_line (
  order_id    INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(order_id),
  line_number INTEGER NOT NULL,
  sku         TEXT NOT NULL,
  quantity    INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0),
  unit_price  NUMERIC(10,2) NOT NULL CHECK (unit_price >= 0),
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, line_number)
);

INSERT INTO orders VALUES
  (1001, DATE '2026-10-01', 501),
  (1002, DATE '2026-10-01', 502),
  (1003, DATE '2026-10-02', 501);

INSERT INTO order_line VALUES
  (1001, 1, 'MUG-BLUE', 2, 8.00),
  (1001, 2, 'TEA-EARL', 1, 12.50),
  (1002, 1, 'MUG-BLUE', 1, 8.00),
  (1003, 1, 'INFUSER', 1, 6.00),
  (1003, 2, 'TEA-GRN', 2, 11.00),
  (1003, 3, 'HONEY', 1, 5.50);

sections.heading: How the reshaped model answers the original questions
paragraphs: After the reshape, ordinary joins recover the combined view when needed. The parent relationship is not encoded in column names; it is represented by a foreign key and used in a join predicate. PostgreSQL’s documentation describes joined tables as table expressions formed from two input tables and a join condition. The same relational idea applies here: combine orders and order_line where their order_id values match.

The line-level table also makes aggregations less fragile. In the denormalized table, counting units of MUG-BLUE requires checking item_1_sku, item_2_sku, and item_3_sku separately, then remembering to update the query when item_4_sku appears. In the reshaped table, sku is one column and each line is one row.

Using the fixture above, the total units by sku are: MUG-BLUE equals 3 units, TEA-EARL equals 1, INFUSER equals 1, TEA-GRN equals 2, and HONEY equals 1. The total revenue by order is also straightforward: order 1001 is 28.50, order 1002 is 8.00, and order 1003 is 33.50. These results follow directly from quantity multiplied by unit_price on the six child rows.

codeExamples.code:
-- Reconstruct an order with its lines.
SELECT
  o.order_id,
  o.order_date,
  o.customer_id,
  l.line_number,
  l.sku,
  l.quantity,
  l.unit_price
FROM orders AS o
JOIN order_line AS l
  ON l.order_id = o.order_id
ORDER BY o.order_id, l.line_number;

-- Count units by product across all orders.
SELECT
  sku,
  SUM(quantity) AS units_sold
FROM order_line
GROUP BY sku
ORDER BY sku;

-- Expected units_sold from the hypothetical fixture:
-- HONEY: 1
-- INFUSER: 1
-- MUG-BLUE: 3
-- TEA-EARL: 1
-- TEA-GRN: 2

-- Compute order revenue without scanning numbered item columns.
SELECT
  order_id,
  SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS order_revenue
FROM order_line
GROUP BY order_id
ORDER BY order_id;

-- Expected order_revenue:
-- 1001: 28.50
-- 1002: 8.00
-- 1003: 33.50

sections.heading: Diagnostic checklist for repeating groups
paragraphs: Use this diagnostic when reviewing extracts, staging tables, or early dimensional models. The goal is not to normalize everything for its own sake. The goal is to avoid hiding child relationships inside a parent row where keys and constraints cannot describe them.

First, inspect column names. Repeating groups often advertise themselves with numeric suffixes: phone_1, phone_2, item_1_sku, item_2_sku, contact_a, contact_b. A suffix is not automatically wrong; for example, billing_address and shipping_address may be two distinct roles rather than a repeating group. The question is whether the columns contain the same kind of fact repeated by position.

Second, ask what the smallest identifiable fact is. If the table is one row per order, but several columns describe individual products, the table is carrying two grains. Write both grains down before changing the schema. If you cannot name the child grain, the split will likely be unstable.

Third, preserve the parent key. A repeating group normally becomes a child table, not a standalone list. The child table needs the parent identifier plus a discriminator that identifies one child occurrence under that parent. That discriminator could be a source line id, an ordinal line number, an effective timestamp, or another business-approved component. The choice depends on the real entity being modeled.

Fourth, avoid using null columns to mean absent child rows. In the bad order extract, NULL in item_3_sku for order 1001 means there is no third item. That is different from an unknown sku for a real third item. Nulls can be appropriate for missing attributes, but they are a poor substitute for representing variable numbers of children. If an order has two lines, store two child rows.

Finally, decide whether the child order matters. In the example, line_number is part of the key because source line position is useful for identifying a line. If order does not matter, you may still need a child identifier. Do not assume that sku or email address is sufficient unless the business rule says duplicates are impossible within the parent.
bullets: Look for positional suffixes in column names.
Write down the parent grain and the child grain separately.
Carry the parent key into the child table.
Choose a child discriminator that matches the business rule.
Represent absent children by absent child rows, not by a fixed set of null slots.
Treat distinct roles differently from repeated positions.

sections.heading: Tradeoffs and boundaries
paragraphs: This article is deliberately narrow. It does not cover second normal form, third normal form, or whether SQL query results behave as sets or bags. It also does not claim that every downstream table must be fully normalized. Analytical marts sometimes denormalize for usability or performance after the base relationships are understood. That is a separate decision from whether the source concept has a repeating group.

The practical tradeoff is that normalized child tables require joins. That is not a defect; it is how the model expresses a relationship that was already present. The important question is where the relationship should be explicit. In a durable relational model, parent-child relationships belong in keys, foreign keys, and rows, not in repeated column names.

A useful stopping rule is this: if adding one more child of the same kind requires adding one more column, the design is probably not in first normal form for that concept. Reshape the repeated attributes into rows, keep the parent key, and define the child grain before building additional logic on top.

takeaways: Repeating attributes such as item_1_sku, item_2_sku, and item_3_sku hide child rows inside a parent row.
A correct 1NF reshape carries the parent key into a child table and defines a child key such as order_id plus line_number.
Do not split repeated values into an orphan table; without the parent key, the original relationship cannot be reconstructed.
Absent children should usually be absent child rows, not null-filled numbered slots.
The purpose of the reshape is semantic clarity: one table grain for the parent and one table grain for the repeated child facts.

title: Second and third normal forms
description: A practitioner guide to separating partial and transitive dependencies in a hypothetical order-line dataset, with counterexamples and an illustrative relational design.
lead: Second and third normal forms are easiest to confuse when a table mixes order facts, customer attributes, and product attributes. The practical distinction is this: second normal form removes facts that depend on only part of a composite key; third normal form removes facts that depend on another non-key fact. This guide works through a small hypothetical retail order dataset and shows how to separate the two problems without turning normalization into a vague table-splitting exercise.

sections.heading: Start with the key, not the column names
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical retail dataset loaded into a wide order-line table. Each row represents one product on one order. For this example, assume an order cannot contain the same sku twice. Under that business rule, the candidate key is the composite key (order_id, sku). If the business allowed two lines with the same sku on one order, this assumption would fail and a different key, such as (order_id, line_no), would be needed.

The table below is intentionally not normalized. It is useful because it contains both kinds of dependency that practitioners often mix together: attributes that depend on only order_id or only sku, and attributes that depend on a non-key attribute such as customer_id or category_id.

The hypothetical relation is wide_order_line(order_id, sku, order_date, customer_id, customer_name, customer_email, customer_tier, product_name, category_id, category_name, quantity, order_unit_price). The whole row is identified by (order_id, sku), but many attributes do not need both columns to be determined.

The dependency exercise comes before the DDL. Database constraints can enforce primary keys, unique keys, foreign keys, and checks, but they do not discover the business meaning of a column for you. The modeler still has to decide which facts are about an order, a customer, a product, or a line item.
bullets: Candidate key for this worked example: (order_id, sku).
Line-level facts: quantity and order_unit_price depend on the full key because the same sku can appear on many orders, and one order can contain many skus.
Order-level facts: order_date and customer_id depend on order_id, not on the full composite key.
Product-level facts: product_name and category_id depend on sku, not on the full composite key.
Customer and category descriptive facts introduce transitive dependencies once order and product facts are separated.

codeExamples.code:
-- Hypothetical unnormalized starting point for discussion only.
-- Assumption: at most one row per (order_id, sku).
CREATE TABLE wide_order_line (
  order_id integer NOT NULL,
  sku text NOT NULL,
  order_date date NOT NULL,
  customer_id integer NOT NULL,
  customer_name text NOT NULL,
  customer_email text NOT NULL,
  customer_tier text NOT NULL,
  product_name text NOT NULL,
  category_id integer NOT NULL,
  category_name text NOT NULL,
  quantity integer NOT NULL,
  order_unit_price numeric(10,2) NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, sku)
);

sections.heading: Second normal form removes partial dependencies
paragraphs: A partial dependency exists when a non-key attribute depends on a proper subset of a composite candidate key. In the example, the key is (order_id, sku). The attribute order_date depends on order_id alone. The attribute product_name depends on sku alone. Neither needs the complete key.

That is the specific problem solved by second normal form. A relation is in second normal form when non-key attributes depend on the whole candidate key, not merely part of it. If a table has only single-column candidate keys, partial dependency is not the interesting failure mode, because there is no smaller part of a single-column key to depend on. With composite keys, it becomes a common source of update anomalies.

The anomaly is easy to see. Suppose order 1001 has three skus. The customer_id and order_date would be repeated three times. If the order date is corrected, every line for that order must be updated consistently. Product attributes have the same problem from the other side: if a product is renamed, every historical row containing that sku repeats a value that may now disagree with the product table or with other rows.

The second-normal-form decomposition for this example separates the attributes by which part of the key determines them. The order table is keyed by order_id. The product table is keyed by sku. The order_line table keeps the attributes that require both order_id and sku.
bullets: Partial dependency: order_id determines order_date and customer_id, while order_id is only part of (order_id, sku).
Partial dependency: sku determines product_name and category_id, while sku is only part of (order_id, sku).
Not a partial dependency: (order_id, sku) determines quantity because quantity is specific to that product on that order.
Not a partial dependency: (order_id, sku) determines order_unit_price if the column means the price charged for that order line.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative 2NF-oriented split, before addressing transitive dependencies.
CREATE TABLE orders_2nf (
  order_id integer PRIMARY KEY,
  order_date date NOT NULL,
  customer_id integer NOT NULL,
  customer_name text NOT NULL,
  customer_email text NOT NULL,
  customer_tier text NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE products_2nf (
  sku text PRIMARY KEY,
  product_name text NOT NULL,
  category_id integer NOT NULL,
  category_name text NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE order_lines_2nf (
  order_id integer NOT NULL REFERENCES orders_2nf(order_id),
  sku text NOT NULL REFERENCES products_2nf(sku),
  quantity integer NOT NULL,
  order_unit_price numeric(10,2) NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, sku),
  CHECK (quantity > 0),
  CHECK (order_unit_price >= 0)
);

sections.heading: Third normal form removes transitive dependencies
paragraphs: After the partial dependencies are removed, there is still a separate issue. In orders_2nf, order_id determines customer_id, and customer_id determines customer_name, customer_email, and customer_tier. Therefore order_id determines those customer attributes through another non-key attribute. That is a transitive dependency.

In products_2nf, sku determines category_id, and category_id determines category_name. Therefore sku determines category_name through category_id. That is another transitive dependency. These are not second-normal-form problems anymore, because orders_2nf and products_2nf no longer have the original composite key. They are third-normal-form problems.

A practical statement of third normal form is: non-key attributes should describe the key, not another non-key attribute. The more formal version is framed in terms of functional dependencies: for each dependency X determines A, either X is a superkey or A is a prime attribute. For everyday modeling, the useful diagnostic is to ask whether a descriptive column can be changed by updating the entity identified by another non-key column.

The third-normal-form version separates customer and category descriptions into their own relations. The order still records which customer placed the order. The product still records which category it belongs to. But customer_name is stored with the customer, and category_name is stored with the category.
bullets: Transitive dependency in the order side: order_id determines customer_id, and customer_id determines customer_name and customer_email.
Transitive dependency in the product side: sku determines category_id, and category_id determines category_name.
3NF target: each non-key attribute should be about the key of its own relation, not about a different non-key attribute.
Foreign keys preserve the relationship between the separated facts, while primary keys identify each entity.

sections.heading: Counterexamples that keep the model honest
paragraphs: Normalization depends on business meaning, not column names. The same column can belong in different places under different semantics. A common mistake is to move every price-like attribute into products because it seems to describe a product. That is wrong if order_unit_price means the actual price charged on the order line. Discounts, promotions, negotiated pricing, tax treatment, or historical price preservation can make the charged price depend on the whole line key. In this example, order_unit_price stays in order_lines.

A second counterexample is customer_tier. If customer_tier means the customer’s current loyalty tier, then customer_id determines customer_tier and it belongs in customers. If it means the tier used to price the order at checkout, it may be an order fact or even a line-pricing input. Renaming the column to customer_tier_at_order_time would make that semantic choice clearer. Normal forms do not remove the need to define time meaning.

A third counterexample is the assumed key. The whole 2NF diagnosis above relies on (order_id, sku) being a candidate key. If an order can contain the same sku twice, then (order_id, sku) is not unique and cannot be the candidate key. The designer might introduce line_no and make (order_id, line_no) the key. Under that alternative key, sku is no longer part of the key, so product_name is not a partial dependency on sku; it is a transitive dependency from the line key through sku. The final 3NF design may still have a products table, but the reason changes.

These counterexamples are not edge cases. They are the difference between modeling a transaction and modeling the current state of a reference entity. Before decomposing a table, define the grain, candidate keys, and time meaning of each attribute.
bullets: Do not move order_unit_price to products unless it truly means a current product price rather than a charged line price.
Do not treat customer_tier as a customer attribute until you know whether it is current tier or tier at purchase time.
Do not diagnose partial dependencies until the candidate key is valid under the business rules.

codeExamples.code:
-- Alternative key shape when duplicate skus are allowed on an order.
-- In this design, sku is a non-key attribute of the line, not part of the line key.
CREATE TABLE order_lines_with_line_no (
  order_id integer NOT NULL,
  line_no integer NOT NULL,
  sku text NOT NULL,
  quantity integer NOT NULL,
  order_unit_price numeric(10,2) NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, line_no)
);

sections.heading: A diagnostic sequence for separating 2NF and 3NF issues
paragraphs: When reviewing a wide order dataset, use a short dependency pass before designing tables. First, write the candidate key at the top of the page. Second, mark each non-key attribute with the determinant that actually identifies it. Third, classify dependencies whose determinant is a proper subset of a composite key as second-normal-form problems. Fourth, after removing those, classify dependencies where one non-key attribute determines another non-key attribute as third-normal-form problems.

For the hypothetical wide_order_line table, the determinant map looks like this: order_id determines order_date and customer_id; sku determines product_name and category_id; customer_id determines customer_name, customer_email, and customer_tier; category_id determines category_name; and the full pair (order_id, sku) determines quantity and order_unit_price. That map is more useful than a debate over whether a column feels like it belongs to an order or a product.

The normalized design is not automatically the physical design for every analytic workload. Data warehouses often publish denormalized marts for query convenience. That does not invalidate the relational dependency analysis. It means the engineer should know whether a repeated column is deliberate derived data or an accidental source of inconsistent facts.

Joins are how the separated relations are reassembled for use. For example, an analyst can join order_lines to orders, customers, products, and categories to produce the same descriptive view. The important modeling point is that each fact has one authoritative home before it is projected into a wider result.
bullets: Step 1: confirm the row grain and candidate key.
Step 2: list functional dependencies using business rules, not sample coincidences.
Step 3: remove dependencies on part of a composite key to satisfy 2NF.
Step 4: remove dependencies between non-key attributes to satisfy 3NF.
Step 5: keep transaction-specific measures, such as charged price, at the grain where they are true.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative query to reconstruct a wide order view from the 3NF tables.
SELECT
  o.order_id,
  o.order_date,
  c.customer_id,
  c.customer_name,
  c.customer_email,
  c.customer_tier,
  ol.sku,
  p.product_name,
  cat.category_id,
  cat.category_name,
  ol.quantity,
  ol.order_unit_price
FROM order_lines AS ol
JOIN orders AS o
  ON o.order_id = ol.order_id
JOIN customers AS c
  ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
JOIN products AS p
  ON p.sku = ol.sku
JOIN categories AS cat
  ON cat.category_id = p.category_id;

takeaways: Second normal form is about removing non-key attributes that depend on only part of a composite candidate key.
Third normal form is about removing non-key attributes that depend on other non-key attributes.
The same final table split can have different reasoning depending on the valid candidate key, so confirm the key before diagnosing dependencies.
Transaction-specific facts, such as the unit price actually charged, should stay at the line grain when they depend on the full line key.
A normalized source model can still feed denormalized analytic views; normalization defines authoritative homes for facts, not the only shape users may query.

title: Entity identity versus record identity
description: A practical guide to separating a durable business entity from the many records that observe, describe, or reference it, using a small hypothetical retail dataset and counterexamples.
lead: A row is not always an entity. In operational and analytical systems, the same customer, product, merchant, or account may appear in many records: orders, emails, returns, support tickets, address snapshots, and source-system extracts. Treating every record identifier as the identifier of the business entity creates duplicated entities, unstable metrics, and hard-to-explain joins. The fix is to model entity identity separately from record identity.

sections.heading: The core distinction
paragraphs: Entity identity answers the question: which business thing are we talking about? Record identity answers the question: which stored observation, message, event, or row are we talking about?

Those questions often have different answers. A customer entity may have one durable customer_id in a modeled data layer, while the same customer appears in many order records, profile snapshots, email-change events, loyalty-program records, and source-system rows. Each of those records needs its own identity because each is a distinct observation. But none of those record identifiers should automatically become the identity of the customer.

This distinction matters most when a table mixes two grains. A customer profile extract, for example, may look like a customer table because it contains name, email, phone, and address. But if the extract is generated daily, the row represents a daily observation of a customer profile, not necessarily the customer itself. If the same customer appears on Monday and Tuesday, the two rows are two records about one entity.

A useful test is to ask what a key uniquely identifies. If a key identifies a specific load row, message, transaction, or snapshot, it is a record key. If it identifies the business thing across observations, it is an entity key. Candidate keys and alternate keys are still important, but the modeling decision starts by naming the thing being keyed.
bullets: Entity identity is durable across many observations when the business says the thing is the same thing.
Record identity is scoped to one stored row, event, snapshot, transaction, or source message.
A source primary key may be an entity key, a record key, or only unique within one source context. Its name alone does not prove the grain.

sections.heading: A hypothetical retail fixture with two kinds of identity
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical retailer that receives customer profile snapshots from an ecommerce platform and order events from a point-of-sale system. The example is intentionally small so the identity errors are visible.

The profile snapshot table has one row per source extraction of a customer profile. The order table has one row per order. Neither table, by itself, proves the final enterprise customer identity. Each table is an observation source.
Here is the hypothetical data in plain relational form:
bullets: customer_profile_snapshot.source_customer_id is stable inside the ecommerce platform, but the table has multiple snapshots per source customer.
pos_order.pos_buyer_token is a token captured at checkout. It can repeat across orders, but it is not guaranteed to be the enterprise customer identifier.
email is an observed attribute. It can help match records, but it can change, be shared, or be missing.

codeExamples.code:
-- Hypothetical example data. This is illustrative SQL, not evidence of execution.

customer_profile_snapshot
snapshot_id | source_system | source_customer_id | observed_at | email              | full_name
------------+---------------+--------------------+-------------+--------------------+----------
S1          | ecommerce     | C100               | 2026-01-01  | alex@example.com   | Alex Rao
S2          | ecommerce     | C100               | 2026-02-01  | alex@example.com   | Alex Rao
S3          | ecommerce     | C100               | 2026-03-01  | alex.new@example.com | Alex Rao
S4          | ecommerce     | C200               | 2026-01-15  | sam@example.com    | Sam Lee
S5          | ecommerce     | C300               | 2026-01-20  | family@example.com | Jordan Kim
S6          | ecommerce     | C301               | 2026-01-20  | family@example.com | Taylor Kim

pos_order
order_id | source_system | pos_buyer_token | ordered_at  | email_at_checkout  | amount
---------+---------------+-----------------+-------------+--------------------+-------
O10      | pos           | T9              | 2026-01-05  | alex@example.com   | 40.00
O11      | pos           | T9              | 2026-02-10  | alex@example.com   | 35.00
O12      | pos           | T8              | 2026-03-12  | alex.new@example.com | 25.00
O13      | pos           | T7              | 2026-01-25  | family@example.com | 60.00

sections.heading: Counterexamples that break naive models
paragraphs: A naive design might declare snapshot_id as the customer identifier because it is unique in the profile table. That fails immediately: S1, S2, and S3 are three records about the same source customer C100. If snapshot_id becomes customer_id, Alex is counted as three customers before considering orders at all.

Another naive design might use email as the customer identifier. That also fails in both directions. Alex changes from alex@example.com to alex.new@example.com, so one person can have two emails over time. Meanwhile, Jordan and Taylor share family@example.com, so one email can refer to more than one person. Email can be a useful observed attribute or matching signal, but the fixture shows why it is unsafe as the sole entity key.

A third naive design might use the POS buyer token as the customer identifier. In the example, T9 links two orders, but T8 appears when Alex uses a different checkout context. If the model treats token as the durable entity key, order O12 is separated from the earlier Alex orders even though the profile evidence suggests a relationship through the changed email history of C100.

These are not exotic edge cases. They are ordinary consequences of confusing observations with entities. A record can be true and still not identify the entity. S3 truthfully records that source customer C100 had alex.new@example.com on 2026-03-01. O12 truthfully records that an order used alex.new@example.com at checkout. The modeling question is whether those observations point to an already-known business entity, create a new one, or remain unresolved.
A clean model does not pretend the answer is inside one column. It gives records their own keys, entities their own keys, and identity assertions a place to live.
bullets: Unique row does not mean unique entity.
Repeated attribute does not mean shared entity.
Changed attribute does not mean changed entity.
A source identifier may be durable only within the boundary of one system.

sections.heading: A practical relational pattern
paragraphs: A practical pattern is to separate three concerns: raw observations, durable entities, and the evidence that links observations to entities. This avoids forcing every incoming row to be the customer record.

In the modeled layer, customer_entity represents the business entity. It gets a surrogate or durable internal identifier whose job is to group observations that the business currently treats as the same customer. The profile snapshot and order records keep their own record identifiers. A bridge or assertion table records which observed identifiers have been associated with which entity, under what rule, and during what period if needed.
For the hypothetical fixture, one possible modeled result is below. This is not the only valid answer; it depends on business rules. The point is the separation of concerns.

In this modeled result, E1 is the customer entity for Alex. It is linked to ecommerce source customer C100 and to two POS buyer tokens, T9 and T8, because the hypothetical identity rule accepts the ecommerce email-change history as sufficient evidence to connect the checkout emails. E2 and E3 remain separate customer entities for Jordan and Taylor even though they share an email, because the business rule does not collapse shared household email addresses into one person. O13 can be unresolved, linked to a household entity in a different model, or assigned only after stronger evidence arrives. The example below leaves it unresolved at the person-customer level.

This pattern also preserves explainability. If someone asks why O12 is attributed to E1, the answer is not hidden in a destructive merge of rows. It is represented as an assertion that can include source, rule, confidence, and dates. If the rule changes, the model can revise the assertion without rewriting the meaning of the original order record.
bullets: Record tables preserve what was observed.
Entity tables represent the business thing being modeled.
Assertion or bridge tables document why a record or source identifier maps to an entity.
Unresolved records are allowed; they are better than fabricated certainty.

codeExamples.code:
-- Hypothetical modeled layer. Illustrative only.

customer_entity
customer_entity_id | entity_type
-------------------+------------
E1                 | person_customer
E2                 | person_customer
E3                 | person_customer

customer_identity_assertion
assertion_id | customer_entity_id | id_domain                  | observed_id             | rule_name                         | assertion_status
-------------+--------------------+----------------------------+-------------------------+-----------------------------------+-----------------
A1           | E1                 | ecommerce.source_customer_id | C100                  | source_customer_id_is_stable       | active
A2           | E1                 | pos.pos_buyer_token          | T9                    | checkout_email_matches_known_email | active
A3           | E1                 | pos.pos_buyer_token          | T8                    | checkout_email_matches_email_history | active
A4           | E2                 | ecommerce.source_customer_id | C300                  | source_customer_id_is_stable       | active
A5           | E3                 | ecommerce.source_customer_id | C301                  | source_customer_id_is_stable       | active

-- O13 is intentionally not mapped to E2 or E3 by email alone.

sections.heading: Diagnostic queries for grain confusion
paragraphs: Before designing the final identity model, run diagnostics that show whether a proposed key behaves like an entity key or a record key. These queries do not prove business identity, but they expose contradictions that should prevent premature key selection.

The first diagnostic checks whether a supposed entity identifier appears in multiple records. Multiple rows are not automatically wrong; they may be expected. The important point is to name the grain. If source_customer_id has multiple snapshots, then a table keyed by snapshot_id is not a customer entity table. It is a profile observation table.

The second diagnostic checks whether a proposed natural key, such as email, maps to multiple source customers. That result does not mean the data is bad. It means email alone is not a safe customer entity key under this fixture.

The third diagnostic checks whether an order attribution join would duplicate facts. If a join from orders to profile snapshots on email returns multiple profile rows for one order, the join has crossed from entity logic into observation history without choosing the intended observation. This is a relational modeling issue, not merely a performance issue.

The expected results for the fixture are straightforward. source_customer_id C100 has three snapshots. family@example.com appears for two ecommerce source customers. Order O10 and O11 would each match both S1 and S2 if joined to snapshots by alex@example.com without a date rule, duplicating order amounts in an aggregate. O13 would match both S5 and S6 by family@example.com, creating ambiguous attribution.
bullets: Look for repeated records per proposed entity key.
Look for one observed attribute pointing to multiple proposed entities.
Look for joins that multiply facts because they join observations instead of resolved entities.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative diagnostics, not evidence of execution.

-- 1. Does a proposed source customer identifier have multiple observation records?
select source_customer_id, count(*) as snapshot_count
from customer_profile_snapshot
group by source_customer_id
having count(*) > 1;

-- Expected from the fixture:
-- C100 | 3

-- 2. Does email behave as a one-to-one customer key?
select email, count(distinct source_customer_id) as source_customer_count
from customer_profile_snapshot
where email is not null
group by email
having count(distinct source_customer_id) > 1;

-- Expected from the fixture:
-- family@example.com | 2

-- 3. Would a direct email join duplicate or ambiguously attribute orders?
select o.order_id, count(*) as matching_profile_rows
from pos_order o
join customer_profile_snapshot s
  on s.email = o.email_at_checkout
group by o.order_id
having count(*) > 1;

-- Expected from the fixture:
-- O10 | 2
-- O11 | 2
-- O13 | 2

sections.heading: Design rules and tradeoffs
paragraphs: The main design rule is simple: do not let the arrival format decide entity identity. Source records arrive at the grain that is convenient for the producing system. A data model should make its own grain explicit.

A second rule is to preserve the original record identity even after resolution. If a profile snapshot is merged into a customer entity, keep snapshot_id. If an order is attributed to a customer entity, keep order_id. Analysts and engineers still need to audit the observation, reverse an assertion, handle late-arriving data, and explain metric changes.

A third rule is to model uncertainty rather than hiding it. If the business rule says a shared email is not enough to merge two person customers, then the model should allow an unresolved order or a lower-confidence assertion. Forcing every record into exactly one customer entity may make dashboards look complete while making them less trustworthy.

There are tradeoffs. A separate identity assertion table adds joins and governance responsibilities. Someone must define rule precedence, survivorship, conflict handling, and whether deleted or superseded assertions remain queryable. The payoff is that entity identity becomes an explicit model concept instead of an accidental side effect of whichever source table was loaded first.

This article intentionally stays at the relational semantics level. Physical tuning, indexing, and execution plans are separate concerns. The logical requirement comes first: know whether each row represents an entity or an observation about an entity. Once that is clear, performance work has a stable target.
bullets: Choose the entity grain before choosing the entity key.
Keep record keys even when records are resolved to entities.
Represent identity assertions as data when the relationship is inferred rather than inherent.
Permit unresolved and ambiguous observations when the available evidence is insufficient.

sections.heading: A short decision checklist
paragraphs: When reviewing a table, ask four questions. First, what real-world thing or event does one row represent? Second, can the same business entity appear in more than one row? Third, can the proposed entity key change, repeat, or be absent? Fourth, what evidence justifies linking this record to that entity?

If the row is one extraction, event, message, or transaction, give it a record identity. If the business thing persists across those rows, give that thing a separate entity identity. If the connection between them is inferred, store the assertion separately enough that it can be explained and revised.
That separation is the difference between a model that merely stores records and a model that represents the business entities those records describe.

takeaways: Entity identity and record identity answer different questions: what business thing is this, versus which stored observation is this?
A unique row key, source primary key, or repeated attribute should not automatically become the enterprise entity key.
Use diagnostics to find grain confusion, especially joins that duplicate facts or attributes that map to multiple proposed entities.
A robust relational design keeps observation records, durable entities, and identity assertions separate enough to audit and revise.

title: Optional relationships in data models
description: A practical guide to representing absent relationships in relational models without inventing default customers, employees, stores, or other fake entities.
lead: Optional relationships are common: an order might not have a sales representative, a support case might not be linked to a known customer, and a shipment might not have a return authorization. The modeling mistake is to hide that absence behind a fabricated default entity such as employee 0, customer -1, or store UNKNOWN. A better model lets the relationship be absent while preserving the integrity of real entities.

sections.heading: The problem with default entities
paragraphs: Practitioners often reach for fabricated rows when a relationship is optional. The employee table gets an employee named Unassigned. The customer table gets a customer named Anonymous. The store table gets a store named Online Unknown. Those rows make foreign key columns non-null, but they also turn absence into a fake business object.

That tradeoff is usually not worth it. A fabricated entity can be counted, grouped, joined, assigned attributes, and accidentally treated as real. If employee_id 0 means no sales representative, every query that touches employees now needs special handling. If a future analyst forgets the exception, the model answers a different question than intended.

The issue is not whether a column can contain null in every circumstance. The issue is whether the data model distinguishes two ideas that are different: a real related entity, and no related entity. A foreign key value should identify a real row in the referenced table. If there is no such row because the relationship is absent, do not invent one just to satisfy a shape preference.
bullets: Use a real foreign key value when a real related entity exists.
Use absence in the relationship when no related entity exists.
Do not add fake dimension rows merely to avoid nulls or missing association rows.
If unknown, not applicable, and not yet collected are materially different states, model those states explicitly rather than overloading a fake entity.

sections.heading: Hypothetical retail example
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical retail order model. An order is always placed through a channel. Some orders are helped by a sales associate, but many self-service web orders are not. The relationship between order and sales associate is optional. The sales associate itself is not optional when the relationship exists: any associate_id stored on an order should point to a real associate.

Here is an illustrative PostgreSQL 18-style schema. The point is relational structure, not engine tuning. PostgreSQL documentation describes primary key, foreign key, check, and other constraints; this example uses those constraint concepts to express the allowed shape of the data.

codeExamples.code:
INSERT INTO sales_channel (channel_code, channel_name) VALUES
    ('WEB', 'Website'),
    ('STORE', 'Store'),
    ('PHONE', 'Phone');

INSERT INTO sales_associate (associate_id, associate_name) VALUES
    (101, 'Rina Shah'),
    (102, 'Marco Lee');

INSERT INTO retail_order (order_id, order_date, channel_code, associate_id, order_total) VALUES
    (1, DATE '2026-10-01', 'WEB',   NULL, 45.00),
    (2, DATE '2026-10-01', 'STORE', 101, 120.00),
    (3, DATE '2026-10-02', 'PHONE', 102, 80.00),
    (4, DATE '2026-10-02', 'WEB',   NULL, 35.00),
    (5, DATE '2026-10-03', 'STORE', NULL, 60.00);

sections.heading: Read the null as relationship absence
paragraphs: In this model, retail_order.associate_id is nullable because the relationship from an order to a sales associate is optional. The null does not describe an associate. It says the order row does not currently reference an associate row.

That distinction matters in queries. If the question is total order value by associate, the self-service orders should not be grouped under a fake person. They should either be excluded from an associate-specific report or shown as a separate absence category created by the query result, not by the entity table.

The following query is illustrative. It uses a left join so orders without an associate remain visible. PostgreSQL documentation describes joined table behavior, including outer joins, where unmatched rows from the preserved side are still returned with nulls for the other side.

codeExamples.code:
SELECT
    o.order_id,
    o.channel_code,
    o.order_total,
    a.associate_name
FROM retail_order AS o
LEFT JOIN sales_associate AS a
    ON a.associate_id = o.associate_id
ORDER BY o.order_id;

sections.heading: Worked results
paragraphs: For the hypothetical data above, the left join should return five orders. Orders 1 and 4 are web orders with no associate. Order 5 is a store order where no associate was recorded. Those are all absent relationships, but they may not mean the same business state. The model preserves the absence; downstream rules can decide whether to label them self-service, missing attribution, or something else.

The expected result of the illustrative query is: order 1 has channel WEB, total 45.00, and no associate_name; order 2 has channel STORE, total 120.00, and Rina Shah; order 3 has channel PHONE, total 80.00, and Marco Lee; order 4 has channel WEB, total 35.00, and no associate_name; order 5 has channel STORE, total 60.00, and no associate_name.

Now compute totals. Overall revenue is 45.00 + 120.00 + 80.00 + 35.00 + 60.00 = 340.00. Revenue attached to a known associate is 120.00 + 80.00 = 200.00. Revenue with no associate relationship is 45.00 + 35.00 + 60.00 = 140.00. Because absence is represented directly, these figures are not polluted by a fabricated employee row.

codeExamples.code:
SELECT
    CASE
        WHEN o.associate_id IS NULL THEN 'no associate relationship'
        ELSE 'known associate relationship'
    END AS associate_relationship_state,
    COUNT(*) AS order_count,
    SUM(o.order_total) AS order_total
FROM retail_order AS o
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

sections.heading: Counterexample: the fabricated associate
paragraphs: Now compare the same fixture with a common anti-pattern: add associate_id 0 to sales_associate and use it whenever an order has no associate. This satisfies a non-null foreign key design, but it corrupts the meaning of the associate table. The table now contains both people and a control value.

The fabricated row causes practical failures. A headcount query can count one extra associate. An assignment workflow can display Unassigned as if it were selectable staff. A data quality rule that checks every order has a valid associate will pass, even though the business relationship is still absent. A slowly changing employee model, territory assignment, payroll export, or quota model may later inherit the fake row and require defensive filters everywhere.

The deeper problem is dependency. The facts about an order depend on the order. The facts about an associate depend on a real associate. A fake associate row mixes a relationship state into the entity table. Normalization guidance commonly emphasizes organizing attributes around the keys they depend on; putting not applicable or no relationship inside a referenced entity table works against that principle.

codeExamples.code:
-- Counterexample only: do not use a fake associate to mean absence.
INSERT INTO sales_associate (associate_id, associate_name)
VALUES (0, 'Unassigned');

-- This hides absence behind a fake entity.
-- The order now appears to reference an associate, but it does not.
UPDATE retail_order
SET associate_id = 0
WHERE associate_id IS NULL;

sections.heading: When to use null versus an association table
paragraphs: A nullable foreign key is usually appropriate when one row may reference zero or one row of another table. In the example, each order can have at most one current sales associate attribution, so retail_order.associate_id works as a nullable foreign key.

When the relationship itself has attributes, history, multiple participants, or a separate lifecycle, use an association table instead. Absence is then represented by no association row. For example, suppose an order can be reviewed by zero, one, or many fraud reviewers, and each review has a decision timestamp. Do not add reviewer_id_1, reviewer_id_2, or fake reviewer rows to the order. Model the review relationship as its own table.

The following design represents optional review relationships without default reviewers. An order with no fraud review has no row in order_fraud_review. An order with two reviews has two rows. A reviewer_id, when present, must identify a real reviewer.

codeExamples.code:
-- Orders without reviews are found by the absence of association rows.
SELECT o.order_id
FROM retail_order AS o
LEFT JOIN order_fraud_review AS r
    ON r.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE r.order_id IS NULL
ORDER BY o.order_id;

sections.heading: Diagnostic questions for optional relationships
paragraphs: When a model contains values like 0, -1, UNKNOWN, N/A, Not Provided, or Unassigned in a referenced entity table, pause before accepting them. Some special values are legitimate domain members, but many are relationship states disguised as entities.

A useful diagnostic is to ask what would be true if the row were real. Can this customer place a future order? Can this employee transfer departments? Can this store close, move, or have inventory? Can this reviewer sign in? If the answer is no, the row probably does not belong in the entity table.

Also ask whether absence and unknown should be separated. If the business needs to distinguish no associate needed from associate should have been captured but was missing, add an explicit status or reason near the relationship. Do not solve that with two fake associates named No Associate Needed and Missing Associate. Those labels are not people.

For the hypothetical retail order, one possible extension is a reason column constrained to a small set of relationship states. This is only appropriate if the states are part of the business process and are maintained consistently.
bullets: If the related thing is real, store its key and enforce the foreign key.
If there is no related thing, allow the relationship to be absent.
If the reason for absence matters, model the reason as an attribute of the relationship or referencing row, not as a fake referenced entity.
If the relationship can repeat or has its own facts, move it to an association table.
If reports need a display label such as Unassigned, create that label in the reporting query or semantic layer rather than in the entity table.

codeExamples.code:
-- Optional extension for the hypothetical order table.
-- This distinguishes selected absence states without inventing associates.
ALTER TABLE retail_order
ADD COLUMN associate_relationship_reason text NULL,
ADD CONSTRAINT retail_order_associate_reason_check
CHECK (
    (associate_id IS NOT NULL AND associate_relationship_reason IS NULL)
    OR
    (associate_id IS NULL AND associate_relationship_reason IN (
        'self_service',
        'not_captured',
        'not_applicable'
    ))
);

sections.heading: A practical modeling rule
paragraphs: Model optional relationships directly. For a zero-or-one relationship, use a nullable foreign key when the relationship is absent and a valid key when it exists. For a zero-or-many relationship, use an association table and let no row mean no relationship. In both cases, keep referenced entity tables reserved for real entities.

This rule keeps joins honest. Inner joins naturally return rows that have the relationship. Left joins let you keep base rows while showing the optional relationship when it exists. Anti-joins or left joins with a null filter can find rows without a relationship. These query patterns are clearer when absence has not been hidden inside a fabricated default row.

There are tradeoffs. Nullable foreign keys require query authors to understand outer joins and null-aware filters. Association tables require another join. Explicit reason columns require governance so their values remain meaningful. Those costs are usually smaller than the long-term cost of mixing real entities with placeholders that every downstream system must remember to exclude.

takeaways: Do not fabricate default entities such as customer 0 or employee Unassigned just to avoid optional foreign keys.
Use a nullable foreign key for an optional zero-or-one relationship, and use an association table when the optional relationship can repeat or has its own attributes.
If the reason for absence matters, model that reason explicitly near the relationship instead of encoding it as a fake row in the referenced entity table.
Outer joins, grouped labels, and anti-join diagnostics are query-time tools for working with absent relationships; they should not be replaced by polluted entity tables.
